subject: Algorithms & Complexity

blurb: Not just what the algorithm is, but what it costs and why it terminates.

sections.title: What Makes a Procedure an Algorithm
sections.body:
A recipe, a set of directions and a sorting routine are all **procedures**, but only some of them are **algorithms**. Three properties decide it: every step must be **definite** (unambiguous, with no room for judgement), the whole procedure must be **finite** (it halts on every legal input), and every step must be **effective** (a real operation the executor can actually carry out).

Finiteness is the one that bites. Euclid's `gcd` halts because the remainder `a % b` is strictly smaller than `b`, so the second argument is a non-negative integer that decreases on every pass and cannot decrease forever.

A loop whose guard moves *away* from false is a procedure, but not an algorithm - and no amount of speed matters for something that never returns an answer.

annotations.text: The guard tests b against 0, and b is a non-negative integer that strictly decreases - so it must reach 0. That sentence is the entire termination proof.
a % b is strictly less than b. This one fact is what makes the loop finite; nothing else in the function matters to termination.
n moves away from the guard, not toward it. Without the escape hatch two lines down this would run forever, which is exactly what disqualifies it as an algorithm.

checkpoint.prompt: This counts how many passes of Euclid's loop run before it halts. What does it print? Write both lines.
checkpoint.explain: The pairs go (48,18) to (18,12) to (12,6) to (6,0), so three passes. The second call shows that finiteness includes the case where the loop body never runs at all - zero is a perfectly good step count, and a procedure that halts immediately still halts.

sections.title: Count Operations, Not Seconds
sections.body:
Timing a procedure with a clock measures your laptop, your language and whatever else was running - none of which is a property of the procedure. So we count **operations** instead: how many times the work inside the loop actually happens.

That count is not a single number. It is a **function of the input size**, written $n$ - the length of the array, the number of digits, the count of items. Values do not matter to the count; size does.

`sumTo` below performs $n$ additions for input $n$, so its cost is $n$. The closed-form version does one multiply, one add and one divide however large $n$ gets, so its cost is $3$. Those two functions of $n$ - one that grows, one that does not - are what we are really comparing.

annotations.text: The counter is the point of the example. Every time the body runs we charge ourselves one operation.
Ten times the input, ten times the work: 55 in 10 ops against 15 in 5 ops. The count tracks n exactly.
Same answer, 3 operations, and it stays 3 for n = 100 or n = 100000000. This is the difference a growth function exposes and a stopwatch hides.

checkpoint.prompt: Complete the counter so that `countOps(4)` returns `4` - the number of times the loop body runs.
checkpoint.explain: A counter has to start from nothing and grow by one per unit of work; that is the whole instrumentation trick, turning an invisible cost into a value you can print and compare. Starting at 1, or assigning instead of adding, both silently produce a number that looks plausible and is not the cost.
checkpoint.hint: One blank is where the count starts, the other is how it grows.

sections.title: Big-O Is an Upper Bound on Growth
sections.body:
Once the cost is a function of $n$, only its **shape** matters. **Big-O** keeps that shape and throws away everything else: constant factors and lower-order terms. So $3n + 7$ is $O(n)$, and $2n^2 + 100n$ is $O(n^2)$.

Read $O(f(n))$ as *grows no faster than* $f(n)$ - it is an **upper bound**, not an exact count. That is why $O(n^2)$ is a perfectly true statement about a single loop, just a uselessly loose one; we always quote the tightest bound we can defend.

The shapes you meet first, ordered slowest-growing to fastest:

- $O(1)$ - constant, the cost does not depend on $n$ at all
- $O(\log n)$ - halving, as in repeatedly cutting the input in two
- $O(n)$ - one pass over the input
- $O(n \log n)$ - one pass for each halving level
- $O(n^2)$ - a full pass over the input for every element of the input

annotations.text: Each pass throws away half of what is left, so the step count is the base-2 logarithm of n: 3 for 8, and only 10 for 1024.
The inner loop runs a full n times for each of the n outer passes, so the two counts multiply rather than add.
Prints 8 64. Doubling the array would give 16 and 256 - the linear count doubles, the quadratic one quadruples.

checkpoint.prompt: Two loops run one after the other over the same array of length `n`. Give the tightest Big-O time bound, and justify it.
checkpoint.explain: The loops are sequential rather than nested, so their counts add instead of multiplying: n + n = 2n. Big-O then discards the constant factor 2, leaving O(n) - which is why splitting work into a second readable pass costs nothing asymptotically, while nesting that same pass would have cost everything.
checkpoint.hint: Do the two counts add, or multiply?

sections.title: Time Cost and Space Cost Are Two Different Bills
sections.body:
Every algorithm is charged twice: **time**, the operations it performs, and **space**, the memory it holds beyond the input it was handed. Both are measured the same way - as a growth function of $n$ - and both are reported, separately, because improving one very often worsens the other.

The two reversals below are both $O(n)$ in time. They differ entirely in space: `reverseCopy` allocates a second array of $n$ cells, so it is $O(n)$ **auxiliary space**, while `reverseInPlace` swaps within the array it was given and holds only a fixed handful of variables, so it is $O(1)$.

By convention we count only that **extra** space, never the input itself - otherwise every algorithm that so much as reads an array would be $O(n)$ and the measure would distinguish nothing. What `reverseInPlace` pays instead is that it destroys the caller's array, a real cost that Big-O does not show you.

annotations.text: This one line is the entire space cost: an array that will grow to n cells, held alongside the input.
Two indices and one temporary, however large the array. That is what O(1) auxiliary space looks like.
Prints 1,2,3,4,5 - reverseCopy left the caller's array untouched, which is exactly what those extra n cells bought.

checkpoint.prompt: What does this print? Write both lines.
checkpoint.explain: The n cells that copyAll paid for are precisely what buys the independence: pushing onto b cannot disturb a, because b is a second region of memory rather than a second name for the first. Space here is not wasted, it is spent - on the guarantee that the caller's data survives the call.

guided-practice.prompt: What does this program print? Write all three lines.
guided-practice.explain: Input 100 is more than twelve times input 8 and costs only twice as much - that flatness is the signature of logarithmic growth, and it is visible from three data points without any algebra. Each pass discards half of what remains, so the count is simply how many times you can halve n before reaching 1.
guided-practice.hint: Write down the sequence of values n takes: 100, 50, 25, and so on.

guided-practice.prompt: A cookbook says: **stir until it tastes right, then bake until done**. Name which of the three requirements for an algorithm this fails, explain what a machine executing it could not do, and rewrite one of the two steps so that it satisfies that requirement.
guided-practice.explain: It fails definiteness: `tastes right` and `done` are judgements, not tests an executor can evaluate, so two faithful executions could disagree about when to stop. Notice the procedure is still finite and each step is effective - failing any one of the three requirements is enough, which is why the definition is a conjunction rather than a general impression.
guided-practice.hint: Ask what test the executor is supposed to run at the end of each step, and whether two executors would agree on its result.

guided-practice.prompt: Give the value of `ops` at the moment each outer pass finishes - that is, each time execution reaches the end of the outer loop body.
guided-practice.explain: Each outer pass adds a full inner loop's worth of work, so the total climbs by n per pass and lands on n times n. That is the mechanical reason nested loops multiply while sequential loops add: the inner cost is paid over again for every single outer step.
guided-practice.hint: The inner loop runs to completion before the outer counter moves at all.

guided-practice.prompt: The array has `n` elements. Fill the first blank with how many times the loop body runs, and the second with the Big-O time bound written in the form `O(...)`.
guided-practice.explain: The loop is driven by the array's length and by nothing else, so the count is the input size itself - the values stored in the array never enter the calculation at all. Going from the exact count to the bound is then only a matter of dropping constants, of which here there are none.
guided-practice.hint: The counter starts at 0 and stops the moment it reaches the length.

guided-practice.prompt: Instrument a linear search. Write `countComparisons(arr, target)` which scans `arr` from left to right comparing each element with `target`, and **stops the instant it finds a match**. Return the number of comparisons made. `countComparisons([1, 2, 3], 3)` must return `3`, and `countComparisons([], 5)` must return `0`.
guided-practice.explain: The counter must be incremented before the equality test, because the comparison you are about to perform is itself the work being charged for. The revealing rows are the last two: an absent target costs the full n while a target in position 0 costs 1, so one input size admits a whole range of costs - which is why worst case and best case have to be named separately rather than blurred together.
guided-practice.hint1: Increment the counter first, then test - the test is the operation you are counting.
guided-practice.hint2: A `return` from inside the loop is what makes the scan stop early.
guided-practice.hint3: An empty array never enters the loop, so 0 falls out with no special case.

guided-practice.prompt: Give the tightest Big-O time bound for `countComparisons` from the previous challenge, in terms of `n = arr.length`, and justify it. State explicitly which input produces that cost.
guided-practice.explain: Big-O is an upper bound, so it must hold for the most expensive input of each size - the target being absent, which forces all n comparisons. The lucky case of matching at index 0 costs 1, but quoting O(1) would be a claim the algorithm cannot honour, and a bound that only sometimes holds is not a bound at all.
guided-practice.hint: Which arrangement of arr and target makes the loop run the longest?

guided-practice.prompt: Order these growth shapes from slowest-growing to fastest-growing as `n` becomes large.
guided-practice.explain: The ordering is a claim about behaviour at large n, not at small n - at n = 2 an O(n^2) routine can easily beat an O(log n) one, and the ranking only becomes true as n grows. Each step up the list is a qualitative change in which input sizes remain feasible at all, not a constant-factor slowdown.
guided-practice.hint: Ask what happens to each shape when n doubles: unchanged, plus one, doubled, or quadrupled?

guided-practice.prompt: `cells` counts every array slot this program allocates. What does it print? Write both lines.
guided-practice.explain: `cells` is never reset, so the second line is 9 + 16 rather than 16 - the running total is the point, because space is a bill that accumulates rather than a rate that resets. This routine happens to be O(n^2) in time and in space at once, which is unusual: most algorithms carry two different growth functions for the two costs.
guided-practice.hint: cells is declared outside the function, so the second call keeps counting from where the first one stopped.

exam.prompt: What does this program print? Write all three lines.
exam.explain: The exact count is n + n^2, giving 0, 2 and 20. At n = 1 the two loops cost the same, which is why small inputs cannot tell you which term dominates; by n = 4 the quadratic term already carries 16 of the 20 operations, and that widening gap is exactly what Big-O is reporting when it discards the n.
exam.hint: Count the two loops separately, then add.

exam.prompt: Trace the value of `n` after each pass of the loop, starting from `n = 20`. Give one line per pass, stopping when the loop stops.
exam.explain: `Math.floor` is what guarantees termination on odd values: 5 becomes 2 rather than 2.5, so n is always a strictly smaller integer and can never stall just above 1. Four passes for an input of 20 is the logarithmic shape in miniature - doubling the input to 40 would add exactly one more line.
exam.hint1: Halving 5 gives 2.5, and the floor of that is 2.
exam.hint2: The loop stops as soon as n is no longer greater than 1.

exam.prompt: A loop is measured and found to run exactly `3n + 7` times. Fill in its Big-O time bound, then the constant factor and the lower-order term that Big-O discarded to reach it.
exam.template:
3n + 7  is  O(___)
discarded: the constant factor ___ and the lower-order term ___
exam.explain: Both discards rest on the same argument: as n grows, 7 becomes negligible against 3n, and the factor 3 changes how steep the line is but not that it is a line. Big-O deliberately cannot tell 3n + 7 apart from 1000n, and that blindness is the price paid for a measure that survives a change of machine and language.
exam.hint: One blank is a multiplier, the other is an amount added on regardless of n.

exam.prompt: Give the tightest Big-O time bound for this function in terms of `n = arr.length`, and justify it by saying how many times the innermost line runs.
exam.explain: The inner loop pays its full n cost once per outer pass and there are n outer passes, so the counts multiply to n^2 instead of adding to 2n. The practical consequence is the one worth carrying: doubling the input quadruples the work, so an input ten times larger takes a hundred times as long.
exam.hint: For each single step of the outer loop, how many times does the innermost line run?

exam.prompt: Give the tightest Big-O bound on the **auxiliary space** used by this function in terms of `n = arr.length` - the memory it holds beyond the array it was handed - and justify it.
exam.explain: Only three extra names ever exist - `i`, `j` and `t` - and that number does not move when the array grows a millionfold, which is what constant space means. The input array itself is not charged, because counting it would make every array-reading algorithm O(n) in space and the measure would stop distinguishing anything; note the same function is still O(n) in time, so the two bills genuinely differ.
exam.hint: Count the names the function creates, and ask whether that count depends on n.

exam.prompt: Instrument the standard single-pass maximum. Write `countScans(arr)` which takes the first element as a running maximum and compares every **later** element against it, returning the number of those comparisons. `countScans([3, 1, 2])` must return `2`, while `countScans([])` and `countScans([5])` must both return `0`.
exam.explain: The count is exactly n - 1 for every array of length n, and both zero cases fall out of starting the loop at index 1 rather than needing a guard. This is the cleanest illustration of why input size is the right variable: `[7, 7]`, `[1, 2]` and `[9, 0]` all cost the same, because the cost never once consulted a value - only a length.
exam.hint1: Start the loop counter at 1, not 0 - the first element is the seed, not a comparison.
exam.hint2: An array of length 0 or 1 never enters the loop at all, so no special case is needed.
exam.hint3: Charge the comparison on every pass, whether or not the running maximum changes.

exam.prompt: This should return the number of times the innermost line runs, which is `n * n`. Instead it returns `1` for every `n` above zero. Fix it. `countBody(3)` must return `9` and `countBody(0)` must return `0`.
exam.explain: Assignment overwrites where accumulation adds, so the broken version reports the cost of the final iteration instead of the cost of all of them. Worth noticing: it agrees with the correct answer at n = 0 and n = 1, and a miscounted instrument that passes your smallest test cases is the ordinary way a false complexity claim gets published.
exam.hint1: Compare the assignment in the inner body with the counters written earlier on this floor.
exam.hint2: The body must add to what is already there rather than replace it.

exam.prompt: A colleague says a single pass over an array is `O(n^2)`. Explain why that statement is **not false**, why we nonetheless insist on `O(n)`, and what would be lost if loose bounds were accepted as answers.
exam.explain: Big-O asserts *grows no faster than*, and n genuinely grows no faster than n^2, so the loose claim is true - merely uninformative. We demand the tightest defensible bound because Big-O exists in order to let two algorithms be compared, and if every linear routine may be reported as quadratic then the notation separates nothing and answers no question at all.
exam.hint: Read O(f(n)) literally as a claim about growing no faster than f(n), then ask whether that claim is violated here.

exam.prompt: Which one of these facts about a procedure disqualifies it from being an algorithm?
choices: It allocates a second array of n cells, doubling its memory use.
On some legal inputs its loop never reaches a stopping condition.
It is a hundred times slower than another procedure solving the same problem.
It uses only addition and comparison, never multiplication.
exam.explain: Finiteness is part of the definition, whereas being slow, being memory-hungry or using a restricted operation set are all costs rather than disqualifications. The distinction matters because cost is something you optimise while correctness is something you either have or do not - a procedure that never halts has no cost worth measuring in the first place.

exam.prompt: Select every statement that is true of Big-O notation as introduced on this floor.
choices: It states an upper bound on how a cost grows as the input size increases.
It reports the exact number of operations an algorithm performs.
Constant factors are discarded, so 3n and 500n are both O(n).
It is measured in seconds and therefore depends on the machine.
It can describe space cost as well as time cost.
exam.explain: The two false options are the two standing temptations: reading Big-O as an exact count, and reading it as a duration. It is neither - it is a claim about the shape of a growth function, which is what lets it survive a change of hardware and what lets it apply unchanged to memory as well as to time.

sections.title: Counting What the Loop Repeats
sections.body:
To name a function's complexity you do not time it - you count how many times its **innermost work** happens as a function of the input size $n$. Work that happens a fixed number of times no matter how big the input gets is **constant time**, written $O(1)$: reading `a[0]` costs the same on ten elements as on ten million.

A single loop that visits every element once does its body $n$ times, so it is **linear**, $O(n)$. The reliable move is to put a counter in the body and watch the counter, because the counter is the thing the notation is about.

What matters is the **shape of the loop bound**, not the body. A body that does five additions instead of one still runs $n$ times, and $5n$ and $n$ belong to the same class.

annotations.text: No loop, no recursion: one indexing operation. This is O(1) - the input could be a billion long.
The loop bound is a.length, so the body runs exactly n times. This bound is the whole story.
The counter is the honest measure. Watch it, not the wall clock.
Ten times the input, ten times the steps: 10 then 100. That straight-line relationship is what O(n) means.

checkpoint.prompt: What does this program print?
checkpoint.explain: The counter ends at the array's length because the loop bound is the array's length - that is exactly why the first print grows with the input and the second one does not. Indexing `items[0]` is one operation on an array of 6 or 6 million, which is the difference between O(n) and O(1) made concrete.

sections.title: Loops Inside Loops Multiply
sections.body:
When one loop sits inside another, the inner body runs once for **every pair** of outer and inner steps, so the counts **multiply**: $n$ outer passes times $n$ inner passes is $n^2$. Doubling the input therefore quadruples the work, which is the signature of **quadratic time**, $O(n^2)$.

A triangular nesting - where the inner loop starts at `i + 1` and so shortens each pass - runs $\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$ times. That is half of $n^2$ minus a linear term, and it is still $O(n^2)$: the constant $\frac{1}{2}$ does not change how the curve bends.

The rule to read off the page is short. **Nested loops over the same $n$ multiply, and the exponent is the nesting depth.**

annotations.text: This inner loop restarts from 0 on every outer pass, so it runs n times, n times over.
Starting at i + 1 shortens the inner loop every pass: n(n-1)/2 steps in total.
25, 100, 400 - squaring the input size, exactly as n^2 predicts.
Doubling n multiplied the work by 4. That factor of 4 is the fingerprint of a quadratic.

checkpoint.prompt: Give the time complexity of `hasDuplicate(a)` in terms of `n = a.length`, and justify it by counting the comparisons in the worst case.
checkpoint.explain: In the worst case - no duplicate at all - the comparison runs once for every unordered pair, which is n(n-1)/2 times. That is half a square minus a linear term, and both the 1/2 and the -n/2 are discarded, leaving O(n^2). The early `return true` only helps some inputs, and a complexity class is named by the worst case, not by the lucky one.

sections.title: Halving Gives You a Logarithm
sections.body:
A loop that **cuts the remaining work in half** each pass cannot run $n$ times, because after $k$ halvings only $n / 2^k$ is left. Solving $n / 2^k = 1$ gives $k = \log_2 n$, so the loop runs about $\log_2 n$ times and the function is $O(\log n)$.

That is a startlingly flat curve: a million items need about 20 passes, a billion about 30. The base is left out of the notation because changing base only multiplies by a constant - $\log_2 n$ and $\log_{10} n$ differ by a fixed factor of about 3.32.

The pattern to recognise is **the loop variable being divided or multiplied**, not incremented. `i = i / 2` and `i = i * 2` both give $\log n$ passes, while `i = i + 1` gives $n$.

annotations.text: The loop variable is divided, not decremented. That single character is what makes this logarithmic.
0, 1, 3, 9, 19 steps. A million-fold jump in n costs 19 passes, not a million.
Math.floor keeps the value a whole number, and it strictly decreases while above 1 - which is why the loop terminates.
20 -> 10 -> 5 -> 2 -> 1: five passes for n = 40, and 2^5 = 32 is just under 40.

checkpoint.prompt: Trace `let i = 100;` under `while (i > 1) { i = Math.floor(i / 2); }`. Give the value of `i` after each pass, then the total number of passes.
checkpoint.explain: Six passes for n = 100, and $\log_2 100 \approx 6.64$ - the floor division rounds the count down. Notice how cheap a hundred elements are, and that the flooring at pass 3 (25 becomes 12, not 12.5) never threatens termination, because the value strictly decreases on every single pass.

sections.title: Adding, Dropping and the Dominant Term
sections.body:
Two loops **one after another** do not multiply - their counts **add**. Two passes over the same array is $n + n = 2n$ steps, and $2n$ is $O(n)$, because a constant multiplier does not change the shape of the curve.

When the added pieces have different shapes you keep only the **dominant term**: $n^2 + n$ is $O(n^2)$, since for large $n$ the square swamps everything under it. So $3n^2 + 50n + 700$ is $O(n^2)$ too, however large that 700 looks at $n = 5$.

Two rules finish the floor.

- **Sequential work adds; nested work multiplies.**
- **Drop constant factors, and drop every term but the fastest-growing one.**

annotations.text: n steps from this loop...
...plus n * n from this one. They are sequential, so the counts add: n^2 + n in total.
The ratio to n^2 marches 1.1000, 1.0100, 1.0010 towards 1. The linear term is being swallowed.

checkpoint.prompt: A function does exactly $3n^2 + 50n + 700$ operations. Explain why it is $O(n^2)$, and why that is still the right answer even though $50n + 700$ is far bigger than $3n^2$ when $n = 5$.
checkpoint.explain: Big-O describes behaviour as $n$ grows without bound, not at any one small size. Past about $n = 30$ the quadratic term takes the lead and keeps pulling further ahead, so the lower-order terms and the factor 3 change only where the curve sits, never how it bends. Naming the class is about the shape of growth; the constants belong to benchmarking.

guided-practice.prompt: What does this program print?
guided-practice.explain: Counting is the primitive skill under every complexity claim: one loop gives n, the same loop nested inside itself gives n times n. Six and thirty-six are not just two numbers here - they are the two growth classes you are learning to tell apart at a glance.

guided-practice.prompt: Name the time complexity of `secondLargest(a)` in terms of `n = a.length`, and justify it by counting how many array elements the function inspects and how much work each one costs.
guided-practice.explain: A branching body is still a constant amount of work per element - at most two comparisons and two assignments - so the loop bound alone decides the class. This is the trap the floor is training away: complexity counts how many times a body runs, not how many lines are inside it.

guided-practice.prompt:
Trace `steps` in this triangular nesting for `n = 4`, starting from `steps = 0`. Give the value of `steps` at the end of each outer pass.

`for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) { for (let j = i + 1; j < n; j++) { steps++; } }`
guided-practice.explain: The inner loop shrinks by one each pass - 3, then 2, then 1, then 0 - and 3 + 2 + 1 + 0 = 6 = n(n-1)/2. Watching the increments die away shows exactly where the factor of one half comes from, and why half a square is still a square.

guided-practice.prompt: Fill the blanks so this loop runs in $O(\log n)$ time: it must keep going while `i` is above 1, and shrink `i` by a factor of two on each pass.
guided-practice.explain: Dividing rather than decrementing is the single edit that turns a linear loop into a logarithmic one, and the `> 1` guard is what makes it terminate: `i` strictly decreases while it is above 1, so the loop cannot run forever. Writing `i - 2` in place of the division would give n/2 passes, which is still O(n).

guided-practice.prompt: Write `innerSteps(n)` returning how many times the innermost line runs in `for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) { for (let j = i + 1; j < n; j++) { /* here */ } }`. It must return `0` for `n = 0` and for `n = 1`.
guided-practice.hint: Either simulate the loops, or use n * (n - 1) / 2 - and check the two agree at n = 5.
guided-practice.explain: Both accepted answers - the simulation and `n * (n - 1) / 2` - produce identical numbers, which is the point: the closed form is what the nested loops *are*, and it is where the n^2 in O(n^2) becomes visible. The n = 0 and n = 1 cases matter because a loop that never enters still has a well-defined cost of zero.

guided-practice.prompt: Two functions both process an array of length `n`. One runs two separate loops one after the other; the other runs one loop nested inside another. Explain why the first is $O(n)$ and the second is $O(n^2)$.
guided-practice.explain: Sequential loops finish one before the other starts, so their counts add: n + n = 2n, and the 2 is a constant factor that drops away. A nested loop restarts its whole run for every outer step, so the counts multiply into n * n. The layout on the page - side by side, or one inside the other - is what decides between addition and multiplication.

guided-practice.prompt: Put these complexity classes in order from slowest-growing to fastest-growing.
guided-practice.explain: The ordering is what makes the classes useful: at n = 1,000,000 these cost roughly 1 step, 20 steps, a million steps and a million million steps. Constant beats logarithmic beats linear beats quadratic for every large enough n, which is precisely why the dominant term is the only one worth naming.

exam.prompt: Name the time complexity of `middleThree(a)` in terms of `n = a.length` and justify it.
exam.explain: Reaching the middle of an array is not the same as walking to it: indexing is a single address computation, so three reads cost three steps whatever the length. Constant time means the step count contains no `n` at all - not that the function is short.

exam.prompt: Name the time complexity of `countDigits(n)` for a positive integer `n`, and justify it in terms of how `n` changes on each pass.
exam.explain: Dividing by 10 rather than 2 gives $\log_{10} n$ passes, and $\log_{10} n$ is $\log_2 n$ divided by about 3.32 - a constant factor, which big-O discards, so the base never appears in the notation. Any loop whose variable is divided by a fixed constant greater than 1 is logarithmic.

exam.prompt: Name the time complexity of `report(a)` in terms of `n = a.length`. Your justification must account for both loops.
exam.explain: The two phases are sequential, so their costs add to $n^2 + n$, and then the linear term is dropped because the square dominates it for all large $n$. Deleting the first loop entirely would not change the answer - which is the practical lesson: optimising anything but the dominant term buys nothing asymptotically.

exam.prompt: What does this program print?
exam.explain: Multiplying up to n is the mirror image of halving down from it and gives the same count: `i` takes the values 1, 2, 4 for n = 8, stopping when it reaches 8. Eight times the input cost three more passes rather than eight times as many - that is $\log_2$ read straight off the output.

exam.prompt: Trace a binary search over the 16 indices `0..15` where the target always lies in the upper half of whatever range remains. Start with `lo = 0`, `hi = 15`; each pass computes `mid = Math.floor((lo + hi) / 2)` and then sets `lo = mid + 1`. Give `lo,hi` after each pass, then the number of passes until `lo > hi`.
exam.explain: The window width goes 16, 8, 4, 2, 1, 0 - halving each pass - so sixteen candidates are exhausted in five looks rather than sixteen. The halving is also the termination argument: a width that strictly shrinks and cannot go below zero must reach zero, so the loop provably ends.

exam.prompt: Write `halvingSteps(n)` returning how many times `n` can be replaced by `Math.floor(n / 2)` before it reaches 1 or below. `halvingSteps(1)` is `0` and `halvingSteps(8)` is `3`.
exam.explain: The function you just wrote *is* $\lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$, computed by a loop instead of a formula, and the counts it returns - 19 for a million - are why $O(\log n)$ is treated as almost free. `n = 1` returning 0 is the edge case proving the loop is guarded at the top rather than run at least once.

exam.prompt: Someone claims that `for (let i = 0; i < n; i += 2) { ... }` is $O(\log n)$ because it "skips half the work". Explain what is really happening and give the correct class.
exam.explain: Halving the work **once** is a constant factor; halving the **remaining** work on every pass is a logarithm. This loop runs n/2 times, and n/2 is O(n) - doubling n still doubles the cost, which a logarithmic loop never does. The tell is that `i` is incremented by a constant rather than divided by one.

exam.prompt: Two loops run one after another over the same array of length `n`. Complete the accounting: first the total step count as a multiple of `n`, then the complexity class, writing only what goes inside the brackets of `O(...)`.
exam.explain: Writing the count down before naming the class is the discipline that stops guesswork: 2n really is twice the work of n, yet both are straight lines, so both are O(n). Constants matter to a stopwatch and not to a growth class.

exam.prompt: Which of these runs in $O(n^2)$ time, where `n = a.length`?
choices: for (let i = 0; i < a.length; i++) { for (let j = 0; j < 10; j++) { total++; } }
for (let i = 0; i < a.length; i++) { for (let j = 0; j < a.length; j++) { total++; } }
for (let i = 1; i < a.length; i = i * 2) { total++; }
for (let i = 0; i < a.length; i++) { total++; } for (let j = 0; j < a.length; j++) { total++; }
exam.explain: Only the second nests one n-bounded loop inside another. The first is nested but its inner bound is the constant 10, giving 10n = O(n); the third doubles its counter, giving O(log n); the fourth is sequential, giving 2n = O(n). Nesting alone does not make a quadratic - both bounds have to depend on n.

exam.prompt: Select every statement that is true of $f(n) = 4n^2 + 1000n + 9$.
choices: It is O(n^2).
It is O(n), because 1000n is the largest term when n = 10.
The constant 9 is dropped because it does not grow with n.
The factor 4 is dropped because a constant multiplier does not change the growth class.
It cannot be bounded by n^3, since f has no cubic term.
exam.explain: Big-O is a claim about large $n$, so which term is biggest at $n = 10$ is irrelevant - that is the classic error in the second option. The last option is false too: $O$ is an upper bound, so this function genuinely is $O(n^3)$ as well; $O(n^2)$ is simply the tightest bound, and the tightest one is what we mean when we name a class.

sections.title: Arrays, Swaps, and What We Count
sections.body:
An **array** is a block of slots numbered $0$ to $n-1$, and reading `xs[i]` costs the same whatever $i$ is. Every sort on this floor rearranges those slots using one primitive, the **swap**, which needs a temporary variable because the first assignment would otherwise destroy the value you still need.

A sort is **in-place** when it needs only $O(1)$ extra memory - a few indices and one temporary - instead of a second array. All three sorts here are in-place; `slice()` appears only so the examples leave the caller's array alone.

We do not count seconds, we count **comparisons** and **swaps**. Two nested loops that pair every index with every later index run $n(n-1)/2$ times, and that single fact is where every $O(n^2)$ on this floor comes from.

annotations.text: The temporary is not decoration: without it, a[i] = a[j] would overwrite the value we are about to need.
The outer index stops one short of the end, because the inner loop always looks at a later slot.
The counter and the closed form agree: 6 pairs for n = 4, which is 4 * 3 / 2.

checkpoint.prompt: What does this print?
checkpoint.explain: `b` is another name for the same array, so an in-place write through `a` is visible through `b`. `slice()` built a separate block of slots - exactly the extra $O(n)$ space an in-place sort refuses to pay for.

sections.title: Bubble Sort and the Sorted Tail
sections.body:
**Bubble sort** walks left to right comparing each adjacent pair and swapping when they are out of order. One such pass necessarily drags the largest remaining value all the way to the right end, because once the walk picks that value up, nothing later can beat it.

That gives the **invariant**: after $i$ passes, the last $i$ slots hold the $i$ largest values in their final sorted positions, so the next pass can stop $i$ short. The invariant is also the termination argument - each pass shrinks the unsorted prefix by one, so at most $n-1$ passes can happen.

The `swapped` flag is a genuine improvement: a pass with no swaps proves nothing is out of order, so already-sorted input costs one pass and $n-1$ comparisons. Without the flag, bubble sort is $O(n^2)$ on every input, including a sorted one.

annotations.text: The `- i` is the invariant made executable: the last i slots are already final, so do not look at them.
One swap anywhere is enough to say the array might still be unsorted.
A clean pass is a proof of sortedness, which is why sorted input finishes after one pass.

checkpoint.prompt: What does this print? It performs exactly one pass of bubble sort, logging after each comparison.
checkpoint.explain: Watch 9 travel: it is picked up at j=1 and carried right by every later comparison. That is why one pass always ends with the maximum in the last slot even though the front of the array is still a mess.

sections.title: Selection Sort: Find, Then Place
sections.body:
**Selection sort** scans the whole unsorted suffix for the smallest value and swaps it into slot $i$. Its invariant is stronger than bubble sort's: after $i$ iterations, `a[0..i-1]` holds the $i$ smallest values in sorted order and none of them will ever move again.

The scan is unavoidable - to know the minimum you must look at every remaining element - so the comparison count is $(n-1) + (n-2) + \cdots + 1 = n(n-1)/2$ **regardless of the input**. Sorted, reversed or shuffled, selection sort does the same work, which makes it $O(n^2)$ in the best case as well as the worst.

What it buys is swaps: at most $n-1$ of them, one per outer iteration, which matters when moving an element is far more expensive than comparing two. The price is **stability** - that long-range swap can throw an equal-keyed element behind another one, so selection sort as written here is not stable.

annotations.text: `min` starts at i, so a suffix whose smallest element is already in place still costs a full scan.
Strict `<` keeps the earliest minimum, but the long-range swap below can still reorder equal keys.
Each printed line shows the sorted prefix growing by exactly one permanently final slot.

checkpoint.prompt: Complete the scan that finds the index of the smallest value in the unsorted suffix `a[i..n-1]`.
checkpoint.explain: Starting at `i + 1` is not an optimisation, it is the definition: slot `i` is already the incumbent minimum, so comparing it with itself is wasted work. Using `<` rather than `<=` keeps the leftmost of any tied values as the chosen minimum.

sections.title: Insertion Sort: Shift Into Place
sections.body:
**Insertion sort** treats `a[0..i-1]` as a sorted hand of cards and slides `a[i]` down into place, shifting larger values one slot right as it goes. Its invariant is weaker than selection sort's - the prefix is sorted, but a value in it may still be pushed right later - yet it suffices, because when $i$ reaches $n$ the prefix is the whole array.

The inner `while` stops the moment it meets a value that is not greater than the key, and that is the whole story of the best case: on already-sorted input it stops immediately every time, doing $n-1$ comparisons and zero shifts, so insertion sort runs in $O(n)$ there. On reversed input the key must travel past the entire prefix, giving $n(n-1)/2$ shifts and $O(n^2)$.

Because the guard is a strict `a[j] > key`, an element equal to the key halts the shift and the key settles **after** it - so equal keys keep their original relative order and insertion sort is **stable**.

annotations.text: `key` must be saved first: the shifting loop is about to overwrite slot i.
Two guards. `j >= 0` stops at the left wall; `a[j] > key` stops at the insertion point - and its strictness is what makes the sort stable.
After the loop, j+1 is the first slot the key is not smaller than, whether the loop ran zero times or i times.

checkpoint.prompt: Write `insertAt(sorted, key)` which takes an already-sorted array `sorted` and returns a **new** array holding every element of `sorted` plus `key`, still in ascending order. Use the shifting insertion step from the lesson, not a library sort. Do not modify `sorted`.
checkpoint.hint: Push key onto the end, then let j start at the second-to-last index and walk left while a[j] > key.
checkpoint.explain: This single step is the entire outer-loop body of insertion sort. Notice it does almost no work when `key` already belongs at the end - that early stop, repeated $n-1$ times, is precisely why sorted input costs $O(n)$.

guided-practice.prompt: What does this print? It counts how many index pairs a doubly nested scan visits.
guided-practice.explain: The nest visits every unordered pair of distinct indices exactly once, and there are $n(n-1)/2$ of them. Nothing in the body changes that count, so any algorithm shaped like this is already $\Theta(n^2)$ before a single line of real work is written.

guided-practice.prompt: Trace one full left-to-right pass of bubble sort over `[5, 1, 4, 2, 8]`. For each comparison of `a[j]` with `a[j+1]`, give the array as it stands **after** that comparison has been handled. Write arrays as `[1, 4, 2, 5, 8]`.
guided-practice.explain: The 5 is picked up at the first comparison and carried right until something beats it. That is the mechanism behind the invariant: whatever the walk is carrying at the end is the maximum of everything it walked over, so it lands in the final slot. The front, meanwhile, is still unsorted - `[1, 4, 2]` is the proof that one pass is not a sort.

guided-practice.prompt: Write `bubblePass(xs)` performing exactly **one** left-to-right pass of bubble sort and returning the resulting array. Compare each adjacent pair `xs[j]`, `xs[j+1]` once, swapping when the left one is strictly greater. Return a new array; do not modify `xs`.
guided-practice.hint: The last valid j is a.length - 2, because the body reads a[j + 1].
guided-practice.explain: The empty array is why the bound is written `j < a.length - 1` rather than a hand-counted number: at length 0 the condition is false immediately, so nothing reads past the end. The `[2, 2, 1]` case shows a strict `>` leaving equal values untouched - the seed of stability.

guided-practice.prompt: Put these lines in the order that makes a correct insertion sort of the array `a`.
guided-practice.explain: Two orderings are tempting and both break the sort: saving `key` after the shifting has begun loses the value, and putting `a[j + 1] = key` inside the while loop writes the key down at every step instead of once at its resting place. The outer loop starts at 1 because a one-element prefix is already sorted.

implementation.prompt: Write `bubbleSort(xs)` returning a new ascending-sorted array. Use bubble sort with the early-exit flag: if a pass performs no swaps, stop. Do not modify `xs` and do not call any built-in sort.
implementation.hint: Inner bound `j < a.length - 1 - i`: the last i slots are already final.
implementation.explain: The `- i` saves roughly half the running time and costs nothing, because the invariant has already proved those slots are done. The flag is what separates $O(n^2)$-always from $O(n)$-on-sorted-input, and it is sound because a pass with no swaps proves no adjacent pair is out of order - which, for a total order, means the whole array is sorted.

implementation.prompt: Write `selectionSort(xs)` returning a new ascending-sorted array. On each outer iteration find the index of the smallest value in the unsorted suffix and swap it into place. Do not modify `xs` and do not call any built-in sort.
implementation.hint: Track an index `min`, not a value - only the index tells you what to put back into the slot you vacate.
implementation.explain: Tracking the index rather than the value is the whole trick: the minimum value tells you what to place, only its index tells you what to swap back. Note the already-sorted test runs exactly as slowly as the reversed one - the scan cannot be short-circuited, which is why selection sort has no best case.

implementation.prompt: Write `insertionSort(xs)` returning a new ascending-sorted array using the shift-and-insert method from the lesson. The inner loop must stop as soon as it meets a value that is not greater than the key. Do not modify `xs` and do not call any built-in sort.
implementation.hint: Save the key before shifting; the loop is about to overwrite a[i].
implementation.explain: The `j >= 0` guard is not paranoia - without it a key smaller than everything walks off the front, and `a[j]` is then `undefined`, where `undefined > key` is false, so the loop would stop by accident rather than by design. Note also that the sorted case does one comparison per element and no shifts: the same code that is $O(n^2)$ on reversed input is $O(n)$ here.

implementation.prompt: This insertion sort returns wrong answers. Exactly one line is wrong. Fix it so `insertionSort(xs)` returns a new ascending-sorted array.
implementation.hint: Which direction is the shift meant to go? Read the assignment inside the while loop out loud.
implementation.explain: `a[j] = a[j + 1]` copies leftwards, dragging the gap the wrong way and duplicating whatever sat to the right. The shift must move the larger value **up** into the gap: `a[j + 1] = a[j]`. The already-sorted test still passes with the bug, because the while loop never runs there - which is exactly why sorted input is a useless test for this class of fault.

analysis.prompt: Give the worst-case time complexity of selection sort on an array of $n$ elements and justify it by counting comparisons. Say explicitly what happens to that count when the input is already sorted.
analysis.explain: Selection sort's comparison count is a constant of the algorithm, not of the data: iteration $i$ always scans the full remaining suffix, giving $(n-1)+(n-2)+\cdots+1 = n(n-1)/2$ comparisons. So its best, average and worst cases are all $\Theta(n^2)$ - unusual, and the reason it can never exploit near-sorted data the way insertion sort does. Its one genuine virtue is performing at most $n-1$ swaps.

analysis.prompt: Give the time complexity of insertion sort on input that is **already sorted ascending**, and explain in terms of the inner loop why it differs from the $O(n^2)$ worst case.
analysis.explain: The inner `while` is guarded by `a[j] > key`. On sorted input that very first test fails every time, so each of the $n-1$ outer iterations costs one comparison and zero shifts: $\Theta(n)$ overall. On reversed input the same guard holds all the way to the wall, so iteration $i$ costs $i$ shifts and the total is $n(n-1)/2$. The algorithm never changed - only the data decided which behaviour you got, which is why best case and worst case must be quoted separately rather than collapsed into one number.

analysis.prompt: Sorting `[[2, "a"], [1, "b"], [2, "c"], [1, "d"]]` by the first component, insertion sort yields `[[1,"b"],[1,"d"],[2,"a"],[2,"c"]]` but selection sort yields `[[1,"b"],[1,"d"],[2,"c"],[2,"a"]]`. Define stability, and explain the specific mechanism that makes selection sort unstable here.
analysis.explain: A sort is **stable** when records with equal keys come out in the order they went in. Bubble and insertion sort only ever exchange **adjacent** elements, and only on a strict inequality, so two equal keys are never moved past one another. Selection sort's swap is long-range: sending the minimum to slot $i$ hurls whatever occupied slot $i$ far to the right, jumping it over elements it originally preceded. Here `[2,"a"]` is thrown past `[2,"c"]` on the very first iteration. Stability matters whenever you sort by one field having already sorted by another - it is what makes multi-key sorting by repeated passes work at all.

analysis.prompt: Prove that bubble sort is correct and that it terminates. State the loop invariant maintained by the outer loop, argue that one pass preserves it, and use it to conclude the array is sorted when the loop ends. Then give the termination argument separately.
analysis.explain: The invariant is: before pass $i$, the final $i$ slots hold the $i$ largest elements in sorted order. Maintenance: a pass over `a[0..n-1-i]` compares every adjacent pair, and by induction on $j$ the value sitting at position $j$ after the comparison at $j$ is the maximum of the original `a[0..j]`; at the end of the pass that value is the maximum of the whole unsorted prefix, so it lands in slot $n-1-i$ and the invariant holds for $i+1$. Termination: the outer counter strictly increases and is bounded by $n-1$, so the loop cannot run forever, and the early-exit flag only ever ends it sooner. At exit the invariant with $i = n-1$ says the whole array is sorted. Correctness and termination are separate obligations - a variant that shrank the range only when a swap occurred could still be correct on every input it finished, yet fail to finish.

analysis.prompt: All three sorts on this floor are in-place. Explain what in-place means in terms of auxiliary space, state the auxiliary space of these sorts in big-O, and describe one concrete situation where a sort needing a full extra array would be the wrong choice.
analysis.explain: **Auxiliary** space is what the algorithm allocates beyond the input itself, so the input array does not count against it. Bubble, selection and insertion sort each use a fixed handful of variables - two indices, a temporary, a flag - and that number does not grow with $n$, so their auxiliary space is $O(1)$. A sort needing $O(n)$ extra is the wrong tool when the data already barely fits in memory, on a small embedded device with no heap to speak of, or when allocation itself is the expensive operation. Time, extra space and stability are the three axes of a sorting trade-off, and you rarely get all three at once.

exam.prompt: Selection sort has just finished $i$ iterations of its outer loop on an array of length $n$. Which statement is the invariant it maintains?
choices: `a[0..i-1]` holds the i smallest values in sorted order, and none of them will move again.
`a[0..i-1]` is sorted, but any of those values may still be shifted right later.
`a[n-i..n-1]` holds the i largest values in sorted order.
Every adjacent pair in `a[0..i-1]` is in order, though the prefix may not be sorted overall.
exam.explain: Option 2 is insertion sort's weaker invariant - its prefix is sorted but not final. Option 3 is bubble sort's, which builds the answer from the right end instead. Selection sort's is the strongest of the three: because it always chooses the global minimum of what remains, a placed element is finished forever.

exam.prompt: Written in the standard way shown in this lesson, which of the three sorts is **not** stable?
choices: Bubble sort
Selection sort
Insertion sort
All three are stable
exam.explain: Stability survives only if an element never jumps over an equal-keyed neighbour. Bubble and insertion sort exchange adjacent elements on a strict inequality, so equal keys are never reordered. Selection sort's swap moves an element an arbitrary distance, and that jump can carry it past an equal key that started ahead of it.

exam.prompt: What does this print? It logs the array after each outer iteration of selection sort.
exam.explain: The array is already sorted after the second iteration, yet a third still runs: the outer loop count is fixed at $n-1$ and nothing inside selection sort can detect that it is finished. That is the visible face of having no best case.

exam.prompt: Complete bubble sort with its early exit. `swap(xs, p, q)` exchanges two slots.
exam.explain: The flag must be reset at the top of every pass, not once before the outer loop, or a single early swap would keep it true forever and the exit would never fire. The `- i` encodes the invariant that the last $i$ slots are final, and `break` turns "this pass changed nothing" into a proof that the array is sorted.

exam.prompt: Trace insertion sort on `[3, 7, 4, 9, 2]`. Give the whole array as it stands after each outer iteration `i` completes - that is, once the key has been dropped into place. Write arrays as `[3, 4, 7, 9, 2]`.
exam.explain: Iterations 1 and 3 do a single comparison and stop - the key was already in place. Iteration 4 does the opposite: key 2 walks past all four elements to the left wall, costing four shifts. Sum those per-iteration costs and you have the whole complexity story: cheap when the prefix is friendly, $i$ shifts when it is hostile, $n(n-1)/2$ when every iteration is.

exam.prompt: Give the worst-case number of **swaps** bubble sort performs as a big-O bound, and describe the input that forces it. Contrast it with selection sort's swap count on that same input.
exam.explain: On reverse-sorted input every one of the $n(n-1)/2$ comparisons finds a pair out of order, so bubble sort swaps every single time: $\Theta(n^2)$ swaps. Selection sort on that same input makes the same $n(n-1)/2$ comparisons but at most $n-1$ swaps, because it decides where an element belongs before it moves it. Comparisons and data movement are separate costs, and which one dominates depends entirely on how expensive it is to move a record.

exam.prompt: Explain why all three elementary sorts are $O(n^2)$ in the worst case, arguing from their loop structure rather than by quoting the result. Then say which one escapes that bound on favourable input, and why the other two cannot do the same.
exam.explain: All three place one element per outer iteration and spend up to a linear scan doing it, so the nest is $n$ iterations times up to $n$ inner steps: $\Theta(n^2)$. Halving that to $n(n-1)/2$ changes nothing asymptotically - constant factors do not move a bound. Insertion sort escapes because its inner loop is guarded by the data and can exit after one comparison; bubble sort with the flag gets a similar $O(n)$ on fully sorted input but nothing in between; selection sort cannot escape at all, because finding a minimum requires inspecting every candidate no matter how the data happens to be arranged.

exam.prompt: Write `insertionShifts(xs)` returning the **number of shifts** insertion sort performs on `xs`, where one shift is one execution of `a[j + 1] = a[j]` inside the inner loop. Do not count the final placement of the key, and do not modify `xs`.
exam.hint: Increment the counter in the same place you do the shift - inside the while loop, not once per outer iteration.
exam.explain: The counter you just wrote is the running time made visible. Sorted input gives 0; the reversed five-element input gives $5 \cdot 4 / 2 = 10$, the maximum possible - so one function measures both ends of the analysis. The all-equal case giving 0 is the same strict `>` that makes the sort stable: equal values never move past each other, so they never cost a shift.

exam.prompt: Write `stableSortByKey(pairs)` where each element of `pairs` is a two-element array `[key, tag]`. Return a new array sorted ascending by `key`, with elements sharing a key kept in their original relative order. Use insertion sort; do not call any built-in sort.
exam.hint: The while guard must be `a[j][0] > key[0]`. Using `>=` would shift past equals and destroy stability.
exam.explain: Stability is not something added afterwards, it is one character in the comparison. With `>` the walk halts on the first equal key and the newer element settles to its right, preserving arrival order; with `>=` it keeps walking and lands to the left, reversing every run of equal keys. The three-equal-keys test would still come out sorted under `>=` - it would just read `r, q, p` - which is why stability needs a test of its own and is invisible to a plain sortedness check.

exam.prompt: This bubble sort has an early-exit flag, but it returns arrays that are not sorted. Exactly one line is wrong. Fix it so `bubbleSort(xs)` returns a new ascending-sorted array.
exam.hint: Read the exit condition as a sentence. Which pass proves the array is sorted - one that swapped, or one that did not?
exam.explain: `if (swapped) break` stops after the first pass that did any work, which is exactly backwards: a pass that swapped is proof the array was still unsorted. Only `!swapped` licenses the exit, because a full pass finding no adjacent pair out of order is a proof of total sortedness. Notice the already-sorted and single-element tests pass with the bug intact - a broken early exit is invisible unless your test data actually needs more than one pass.

sections.title: The Sorted Precondition
sections.body:
**Binary search** never looks at the data as a whole - it reads one element and throws away half the array. That is only sound if the array is **sorted**: order is what lets `xs[mid] < target` rule out every slot left of `mid` without reading a single one of them.

So sortedness is a **precondition**, not a preference. On an unsorted array the algorithm still terminates and still returns an answer, and the answer is simply wrong - the worst kind of failure, because nothing crashes.

Each iteration carries a **window** `lo..hi` of slots that could still hold the target, and every probe cuts that window roughly in half.

The search stops in one of two ways: it lands on the target, or the window empties and the target was never there.

annotations.text: lo <= hi means the window still holds at least one slot; lo > hi means it is empty.
xs[mid] < target rules out mid and everything left of it - that discard is the whole algorithm, and only sortedness makes it valid.
Three probes locate 23 among ten values, and three more prove 7 is absent.

checkpoint.prompt: What does this print?
checkpoint.explain: The first probe lands in the middle and 30 is too large, so the entire right half - the middle included - is discarded in one step without being read. Finding the very first element still costs two probes, because binary search never guesses where a value is, it only ever halves.

sections.title: The Invariant and the Midpoint
sections.body:
The **loop invariant** is the sentence that stays true before and after every iteration: *if the target is in `xs` at all, its index lies in `lo..hi`*. Each branch preserves it, because the half being discarded is provably all-too-small or all-too-large.

That invariant is what makes both return values correct. When the loop exits with `lo > hi` the window is empty, so by the invariant the target is absent - and `lo` is left sitting exactly where the target would have to be inserted to keep the array sorted.

The midpoint is written `lo + Math.floor((hi - lo) / 2)` rather than `Math.floor((lo + hi) / 2)`. The two agree in JavaScript, whose numbers are 64-bit doubles, but in a fixed-width integer language `lo + hi` can overflow to a negative index, while the subtracting form never leaves the window.

The property the midpoint really has to guarantee is $lo \le mid \le hi$, together with $mid < hi$ whenever $lo < hi$. Rounding **down** is what supplies it - round up and the window stops shrinking.

annotations.text: The probe never escapes lo..hi - that containment is what guarantees progress.
The loop broke on a hit here; had 11 been absent, lo would have stopped at the insertion point.
In JavaScript both midpoint forms agree, because numbers are 64-bit doubles.
In Java or C the line above overflows to a negative index; this form subtracts first and cannot.

checkpoint.prompt: Fill the blanks so the window shrinks correctly: the probe must round down, and a probe that is too small must discard the left half including mid itself.
checkpoint.explain: `mid + 1` rather than `mid` is what makes the window strictly smaller on every pass - `lo = mid` would leave a two-slot window unchanged forever. Rounding down is the other half of the same termination argument, since it keeps `mid < hi` while the window still has room to shrink.

sections.title: Solving $T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1)$
sections.body:
The cost of one call is a constant amount of comparing plus the cost of searching a window half the size, which is exactly the **recurrence** $T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1)$ with $T(1) = O(1)$.

Unroll it and the shape appears: $T(n) = T(n/2) + 1 = T(n/4) + 2 = T(n/8) + 3 = \dots = T(n/2^k) + k$.

The recursion bottoms out when $n/2^k = 1$, that is when $k = \log_2 n$, so $T(n) = O(\log n)$. The logarithm is not a guess - it is the count of halvings needed to drive $n$ down to $1$.

The base of that logarithm is absorbed by big-O, since changing base only multiplies by a constant, which is why nobody writes $O(\log_2 n)$.

annotations.text: Always taking the right half is the worst case: the window never holds the target and never collapses early.
The measured probe count and floor(log2 n) + 1 agree at every size, a million included.

checkpoint.prompt: Doubling the length of the array adds how much work to a binary search, and why?
checkpoint.explain: Doubling n adds exactly one probe, because a single extra halving takes 2n back down to n. That is the practical meaning of a logarithm - cost grows with the number of doublings rather than with n - and it is why a million-element array costs only twenty probes.

sections.title: The Divide-and-Conquer Shape
sections.body:
Binary search is the thinnest member of a family. A **divide-and-conquer** algorithm splits a problem into $a$ subproblems of size $n/b$, solves them recursively, and combines the results in $f(n)$ time, giving $$T(n) = a\,T(n/b) + f(n).$$

Binary search has $a = 1$ - it recurses into **one** half and abandons the other - with $b = 2$ and $f(n) = O(1)$, so $T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1) = O(\log n)$.

The maximum-finder below keeps **both** halves, so $a = 2$, $b = 2$, $f(n) = O(1)$, giving $T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(1)$. Its recursion tree has $n$ leaves and about $2n$ nodes in total, so the cost is $O(n)$ - recursing does not make a linear scan faster.

When the combine step itself costs $O(n)$ the recurrence becomes $T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n)$: each of the $\log n$ levels does $O(n)$ work in total, so the whole thing is $O(n \log n)$.

The exponent therefore lives in $a$ and $b$, and the extra logarithm lives in $f(n)$ - reading the recurrence tells you the cost before a line is written.

annotations.text: A one-slot window is the base case, and it is what stops the recursion.
Both halves are solved, so a = 2 - unlike binary search, nothing is discarded.
15 calls for 8 elements: 2n - 1 nodes in the tree, which is O(n), not O(log n).

checkpoint.prompt: What does this print?
checkpoint.explain: Four leaves and three internal nodes make seven calls - the $2n - 1$ shape of any recursion tree that keeps both halves. Splitting a sum in half is a legal divide-and-conquer, but with $a = 2$ and $b = 2$ it costs $O(n)$, exactly like the loop it replaced.

guided-practice.prompt: What does this print?
guided-practice.explain: Six elements fall to three probes, and the windows are 6, 3 and 1 slots wide - each probe removes the probed slot as well as the half that cannot hold the target. The last window is a single slot, which is why `lo <= hi` rather than `lo < hi` is what lets the search see it at all.

guided-practice.prompt: Fill the blanks to complete one iteration of binary search over a sorted ascending array held in a closed window lo..hi.
guided-practice.explain: The three blanks are a matched set: a closed window needs `<=` to include its final slot, and both updates must step past `mid`, which has already been compared. Mixing conventions - `<` with `mid - 1`, or `<=` with `hi = mid` - is where nearly every broken binary search comes from.

guided-practice.prompt: Put one iteration of binary search back into the order that preserves the invariant.
guided-practice.explain: The midpoint has to exist before it can be compared, and the equality test has to run before either discard, or a hit sitting exactly on `mid` would be thrown out along with its half. The order is forced by the invariant, not by taste.

guided-practice.prompt: Trace `binarySearch([1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49], 9)`. Give each probe index and the window that survives it, written as `lo, hi`.
guided-practice.explain: Every window here still contains index 2, which is the invariant made visible: the target's index is never outside `lo..hi`. Note the third window is a single slot - the search cannot finish until it has actually looked at it.

guided-practice.prompt: Write `binarySearch(xs, target)` over a sorted ascending array of numbers. Return the index of `target`, or `-1` if it is absent. Probe the middle and discard half the window each pass - do not scan.
guided-practice.hint: The loop condition is `lo <= hi`, and both updates step past `mid`.
guided-practice.explain: The two edge cases are what catch a broken version: a one-element array only works if the loop still runs when `lo === hi`, and an empty array only works if it does not run at all - `hi` starts at `-1`, so the condition is false immediately and `-1` falls out without a single read.

guided-practice.prompt: `binarySearch([9, 2, 7, 1, 5], 1)` returns -1 even though 1 is in the array. Explain what the algorithm concluded, and why sortedness is a precondition rather than a preference.
guided-practice.explain: The first probe reads `xs[2]`, which is 7; since 7 > 1 the whole right half is discarded - and index 3, where 1 actually sits, goes with it. The reasoning 'everything right of mid is larger' is a fact about sorted arrays only, so on unsorted input the discard is unjustified and the failure is silent: it terminates, returns a plausible answer, and never signals that its precondition was violated.

debugging.prompt: This binary search has an off-by-one in its loop condition: it returns -1 for `[7], 7` and for `[1, 3, 5, 7, 9], 9`. Fix it so it finds every present target.
debugging.hint: Ask what the window `lo..hi` still holds when `lo === hi`, and whether the loop ever looks at it.
debugging.explain: `hi` is an inclusive bound, so a window with `lo === hi` still holds one unexamined slot and `lo < hi` walks away from it. The bug hides on most inputs because the target is usually found before the window narrows to one - which is exactly why it survives casual testing and then fails on the last element.

debugging.prompt: `firstIndexOf(xs, target)` must return the index of the **first** occurrence in a sorted array that may contain duplicates, or -1. It currently answers 1 for `[2, 2, 2, 2], 2` instead of 0. Fix it without giving up the halving - a leftward scan from the hit is not a fix.
debugging.hint: A hit is not a reason to stop: record it, then keep searching the left half.
debugging.explain: Returning on the first hit answers a different question - *is it here* rather than *where does it start* - because the midpoint of a run of duplicates is an arbitrary member of that run. Strengthening the invariant to 'best is the leftmost hit seen so far, and any earlier one lies in lo..hi' keeps the cost at $O(\log n)$, whereas a leftward scan would degrade it to $O(n)$ on an array of equal values.

debugging.prompt: A student replaces `hi = mid - 1` with `hi = mid` but keeps the condition `lo <= hi`. Searching for 3 in `[5]` now hangs forever. Explain why, in terms of what each iteration has to guarantee.
debugging.explain: Termination needs a measure that strictly decreases, and here it is the window width `hi - lo + 1`. With `lo === hi === mid`, assigning `hi = mid` leaves the width the same, so the loop repeats an identical state forever. An invariant alone proves nothing about finishing - correctness and termination are two separate arguments, and this change keeps the first while destroying the second.

analysis.prompt: Give the worst-case time complexity of binary search on a sorted array of $n$ elements, and justify it by writing down its recurrence and unrolling it.
analysis.explain: The recurrence $T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1)$ unrolls to $T(n/2^k) + k$, and the base case $n/2^k = 1$ pins $k$ at $\log_2 n$. The logarithm is a count of halvings, so its base is only a constant factor and big-O absorbs it - which is why $\log_2$ and $\log_{10}$ describe the same growth.

analysis.prompt: An algorithm splits its input in half, solves both halves recursively, and spends $O(n)$ combining the results: $T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n)$. Give its complexity and justify it by the work done per level of the recursion tree.
analysis.explain: Level $k$ holds $2^k$ subproblems of size $n/2^k$, so every level combines $O(n)$ in total however deep it sits, and halving bottoms out after $\log_2 n$ levels. Compare $T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(1)$, where the per-level work halves as you descend and the sum collapses to $O(n)$: the extra logarithm is bought entirely by the combine step.

analysis.prompt: Prove that binary search always terminates on any array, sorted or not. Name the quantity that decreases, show it decreases on every iteration, and show it is bounded below.
analysis.explain: The measure is the window width $hi - lo + 1$. Because rounding down gives $lo \le mid \le hi$, both updates - $lo = mid + 1$ and $hi = mid - 1$ - move a bound strictly past $mid$, so the width falls by at least one each pass. It is an integer bounded below by $0$, and the loop condition fails at $0$, so no infinite descent is possible. Notice this argument never mentions sortedness: an unsorted array still terminates, it just answers wrongly.

analysis.prompt: For $n = 64$ in the worst case - the target is never found and the search always takes the right half - give the window width $hi - lo + 1$ after each probe, then the total number of probes.
analysis.explain: This is $T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1)$ written out as data: seven probes for $64 = 2^6$, matching $\lfloor \log_2 64 \rfloor + 1$. The final step from width 1 to width 0 is the base case being consumed - and it is precisely the probe a `lo < hi` loop would skip.

exam.prompt: What does binary search require of its input, and what happens when the requirement is broken?
choices: Distinct elements; duplicates cause an infinite loop
Sorted order; a violation gives a wrong answer with no error
A power-of-two length; other lengths throw a RangeError
Numeric elements; strings make the midpoint undefined
exam.explain: Order is the only precondition, and it is the thing that licenses discarding an unread half. Duplicates and odd lengths are harmless; a violated order costs nothing at run time and everything in correctness, which is why the precondition has to be guaranteed by the caller rather than detected by the search.

exam.prompt: Unrolled, $T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1)$ with $T(1) = O(1)$ solves to:
choices: $O(\log n)$
$O(n \log n)$
exam.explain: Each unrolling step adds a constant and halves $n$, so after $k$ steps the cost is $T(n/2^k) + k$ and the base case is reached at $k = \log_2 n$. The recurrence, not the code, is what fixes the answer - anything with a single recursive call on half the input and constant extra work lands here.

exam.prompt: What does this print?
exam.explain: The loop ends with `lo` one past `hi`, which is what an empty window looks like - and `lo` is 2, precisely where 5 belongs, between 4 and 6. A failed search is not wasted work: it hands back the insertion point for free.

exam.prompt: Fill the blanks so the midpoint takes the form that cannot overflow a fixed-width integer.
exam.explain: `hi - lo` is at most the array length, so adding it back to `lo` can never exceed `hi` - whereas `lo + hi` can approach twice the largest index and wraps negative in a 32-bit language. Rounding down is the second requirement, and it is what keeps `mid < hi` while the window still has room to shrink.

exam.prompt: Order the steps that solve $T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1)$.
fragments: the base case $T(1)$ is reached when $n/2^k = 1$, so $k = \log_2 n$
exam.explain: Unrolling is mechanical: substitute the recurrence into itself, spot the pattern in $k$, then let the base case decide how large $k$ can get. The base case is what converts a pattern into a number - without it the unrolling never stops and no bound ever appears.

exam.prompt: Trace `binarySearch([1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49], 36)`. Give each probe index and the surviving window as `lo, hi`.
exam.explain: Two probes suffice because the second midpoint happens to land on the target - the $O(\log n)$ bound is a ceiling on the worst case, never a promise about a particular search. The invariant holds throughout: index 5 sits inside both windows.

exam.prompt: You run one binary search for each of $n$ queries against the same sorted array of $n$ elements. Give the total worst-case complexity and justify it.
exam.explain: Independent repetitions multiply rather than compose, so $n$ searches at $O(\log n)$ each is $O(n \log n)$. That total is also the argument for sorting first: one sort plus $O(n \log n)$ of searching beats $n$ linear scans at $O(n^2)$, which is why the sort pays for itself as soon as the queries outnumber a constant.

exam.prompt: Write `insertPosition(xs, target)` over a sorted ascending array of distinct numbers. Return the index of `target` if it is present, otherwise the index at which it would have to be inserted to keep the array sorted. Use halving, not a scan.
exam.hint: The ordinary search already computes it - look at what `lo` holds when the loop exits.
exam.explain: The invariant says the target, if present, lies in `lo..hi`; when that window empties, everything left of `lo` is smaller and everything from `lo` onward is larger, which is the definition of an insertion point. Returning `lo` instead of `-1` is a one-token change that turns a failed search into useful information - and on the empty array `lo` is still 0, which is the right answer.

exam.prompt: Explain why the midpoint must round **down**, by describing what a two-slot window does under `Math.ceil` when the update is `hi = mid`.
exam.explain: Rounding down guarantees $mid < hi$ whenever $lo < hi$, so an update that keeps the left side genuinely moves the upper bound. Round up and a two-slot window puts `mid` on `hi`; with `hi = mid` the window is unchanged and the loop repeats forever. Which rounding is correct is not arbitrary - it is fixed by which side the update keeps.

exam.prompt: The recursive maximum-finder splits the range in half, recurses on both halves, and combines with a single comparison: $T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(1)$. Give its complexity and explain why recursing does not beat a plain scan.
exam.explain: With $a = 2$ the recursion tree has $n$ leaves and about $2n - 1$ nodes, and every element must be read before the maximum is known, so nothing can do better than linear here. Binary search is fast because it **discards** a half, not because it divides one - $a = 1$ versus $a = 2$ is the whole difference between $O(\log n)$ and $O(n)$.

sections.title: The Merge Step
sections.body:
Two arrays that are each already sorted can be fused into one sorted array in a single pass: look at the front of both, take the smaller, advance that side. Every comparison emits exactly one element, so merging arrays of length $p$ and $q$ costs at most $p + q - 1$ comparisons and always $\Theta(p+q)$ time.

The two `while` loops at the end are not decoration - when one side runs dry the other still holds elements that are already in order, and they must be copied through.

Taking from `a` on a **tie** (`<=` rather than `<`) is what makes the merge **stable**: equal elements keep the order they came in with.

annotations.text: <= not <, so on a tie the element from a wins. That one character is the whole of stability.
a still has elements, they are already sorted, and they are all larger - copy them straight through.
An empty side means the main loop never ran at all; the drain loops carry the entire answer.

checkpoint.prompt: Write `merge(a, b)` taking two arrays already sorted ascending and returning one new sorted array containing every element of both. Do not call the built-in `sort`.
checkpoint.explain: The drain loops are the part people forget. Once one index reaches the end of its array the main loop stops, and everything still sitting in the other array is already sorted and larger than everything emitted so far, so it can be copied without a single further comparison.

sections.title: Merge Sort Costs the Same Every Time
sections.body:
Merge sort splits the array in half, sorts each half recursively, and merges the two results. That gives the recurrence $T(n) = 2T(n/2) + \Theta(n)$: there are $\log_2 n$ levels of splitting and each level does $\Theta(n)$ work merging, so $T(n) = \Theta(n \log n)$.

The crucial word is **every**. The split is positional, not value-dependent, so the recursion tree has the same shape for sorted, reversed and shuffled input - best, average and worst case are all $\Theta(n \log n)$.

The run below counts comparisons on three arrangements of the same 64 values and stays under $n \log_2 n = 384$ in all three.

annotations.text: The base case. One element is already sorted, and this is why the recursion terminates - every call is strictly shorter than its parent.
The split is by position only. No arrangement of values can unbalance it, which is why merge sort has no bad input.
slice copies. That copying is the O(n) extra space merge sort pays for.

checkpoint.prompt: Write `mergeSort(a)` returning a new array holding `a`'s numbers in ascending order. Split at the midpoint, recurse on both halves, merge the results. Do not call the built-in `sort`.
checkpoint.explain: Without the `length <= 1` guard the recursion never bottoms out and the call stack overflows. That guard is what makes the descent finite: each call halves the length, so after log2(n) halvings you reach a length the base case accepts.

sections.title: Partitioning: Quicksort's Whole Idea
sections.body:
Quicksort does no work combining and all of its work dividing. **Partition** picks a pivot, then rearranges the range so everything smaller sits left of the pivot and everything larger sits right; the pivot is then in its final position forever.

The Lomuto scheme below takes the last element as pivot and keeps a boundary `i`, with everything before `i` known to be smaller. Each `j` step costs one comparison, so partitioning $m$ elements costs exactly $m - 1$ comparisons whatever the data.

After partitioning you recurse on the two sides *excluding* the pivot - that exclusion is what shrinks the problem and guarantees termination.

annotations.text: j stops before hi: the pivot must not be compared with itself, or it could be swapped away from the end.
The final swap drops the pivot onto the boundary. Leave it out and the pivot never reaches its place - a favourite bug.
5 lands at index 3, so 5 is now permanently correct and only the two sides are left to sort.

checkpoint.prompt: Write `partition(a)` that Lomuto-partitions a copy of the non-empty array `a` around its last element and returns `{ index, arr }`, where `arr` is the rearranged copy and `index` is where the pivot ended up. Leave `a` itself untouched.
checkpoint.explain: Partition is not a sort - the two sides come out unordered among themselves. All it guarantees is one element placed correctly and a two-way split, and that single guarantee, repeated, is the whole of quicksort.

sections.title: Pivot Choice and the Quadratic Cliff
sections.body:
Quicksort's cost is decided entirely by how evenly the pivot splits the range. A pivot near the median gives $T(n) = 2T(n/2) + \Theta(n) = \Theta(n \log n)$; a pivot that is always the minimum or maximum gives $T(n) = T(n-1) + \Theta(n)$, which unrolls to $n + (n-1) + \dots = \Theta(n^2)$.

Taking the **last element** as pivot is therefore a trap: on already-sorted input every partition peels off one element, and the run below does exactly $\frac{n(n-1)}{2} = 19900$ comparisons at $n = 200$.

Taking the middle element, or the median of first-middle-last, costs a constant extra per call and removes sorted input as an adversary - though for any fixed rule some input still forces $\Theta(n^2)$.
