So: merge sort when you need a guaranteed bound or stability and can afford $\Theta(n)$ scratch space; quicksort when you want the smaller constant factor and in-place behaviour and can tolerate a rare bad case.

annotations.text: Swap the chosen pivot to the end first, so the Lomuto loop below never has to change.
lo..i-1 and i+1..hi both exclude i, so every recursive range is strictly shorter. That is the termination argument.
Same array, same algorithm, only the pivot rule differs: 19900 comparisons against 1153.

checkpoint.prompt: This quicksort always takes the last element as its pivot, and is handed input that is already sorted. What number does it print?
checkpoint.explain: The pivot is always the largest remaining element, so each partition peels off exactly one element and the ranges shrink by one instead of halving: 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10, which is n(n-1)/2 - the quadratic case in miniature.

guided-practice.prompt: What does this print?
guided-practice.explain: Merging never re-sorts anything: it only ever appends the smaller of the two current heads, so the output order is fully determined by the two inputs already being sorted. After 6 loses to 2 and to 3 it still has to face 9.

guided-practice.prompt: Write `mergeBy(a, b, keyFn)`. Both arrays are already sorted ascending by `keyFn(element)`. Return one new array holding every element of both, sorted by the same key, and **stable**: when two elements have equal keys the one from `a` comes first.
guided-practice.hint: Only two things change from the plain merge: compare keyFn(a[i]) with keyFn(b[j]), and keep <= so ties fall to a.
guided-practice.explain: Stability is not a bonus property merge sort happens to have - it is a consequence of this one comparison operator. Flip `<=` to `<` and equal-keyed elements silently swap order, which breaks any code that sorts by one field expecting an earlier sort by another to survive.

guided-practice.prompt: Complete merge sort. The blanks are, in order: the largest length that needs no sorting, the number the length is divided by to find the midpoint, and the function that recombines the two sorted halves.
guided-practice.explain: Dividing by 2 is what turns the recursion depth into log2(n); dividing by 1 would never shrink the problem and peeling off one element at a time would give n levels. The base case at length 1 is the only reason the descent stops at all.

guided-practice.prompt: `mergeSort([8, 3, 5, 1, 9, 2])` splits at `mid = Math.floor(6 / 2) = 3`, recurses on the left half before the right, and merges on the way back up. Five merges happen in all. Give the array each merge returns, in the order the merges complete. Write arrays as `[1,2,3]`.
guided-practice.explain: The merges complete bottom-up and left-first: the whole left half is finished before the right half is touched at all, because the left recursive call must return before the right one is even entered. Nothing merges until the recursion has bottomed out beneath it.

guided-practice.prompt: Write `quickSort(a)` returning a new array with `a`'s numbers ascending. Copy the array, then Lomuto-partition each range around its last element and recurse on the two sides, excluding the pivot. Do not call the built-in `sort`.
guided-practice.hint: `if (lo >= hi) return;` covers both the empty range and the single element, which is also what makes an empty input safe, since hi is then -1.
guided-practice.explain: The `[3,3,3]` case is the one that catches people: with `arr[j] < pivot` no equal element ever moves, the pivot lands at the far left of the range, and the recursion still shrinks only because the pivot index is excluded. Recursing on `lo..p` instead of `lo..p-1` would spin forever right here.

guided-practice.prompt: Give the worst-case running time of merge sort on an array of $n$ elements, and justify it from the recurrence. Say why no input can do worse.
guided-practice.explain: The recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Theta(n) has log2(n) levels with Theta(n) merging work at each, so the total is Theta(n log n). The reason there is no bad input is structural: the split is by index, so no arrangement of values can make the recursion tree lopsided - unlike quicksort, where the values themselves choose the shape of the tree.

guided-practice.prompt: Merge sort runs in $\Theta(n \log n)$ time but also needs $\Theta(n)$ extra space, while quicksort sorts in place. Explain what specifically about the merge step forces that extra space, and why the recursion depth is not the dominant term.
guided-practice.explain: A merge cannot write its output over its own inputs: the next value it needs might still be sitting in the cell it is about to overwrite. So it needs somewhere else to build the result, and the top-level merge alone handles all n elements. The recursion stack is only Theta(log n) frames deep, which is swamped by that Theta(n) buffer.

guided-practice.prompt: Put one call to `mergeSort(a)` in the order its steps execute.
fragments: Merge the two sorted halves into one sorted array and return it
Split the array at its midpoint into a left half and a right half
Return the array unchanged if it holds fewer than two elements
guided-practice.explain: The base-case test has to come first or the recursion never terminates, and the merge has to come last because it needs both halves already sorted. Everything expensive in merge sort happens on the way back up the tree, which is exactly the opposite of quicksort.

implementation.prompt: An **inversion** is a pair of indices $i < j$ with `a[i] > a[j]`. Write `countInversions(a)` returning how many inversions `a` contains, in $O(n \log n)$ time by piggy-backing on a merge sort. Return a number.
implementation.hint: When you take R[j] while L still has elements from index i onward, all of L[i..] are greater than R[j]. That is `L.length - i` inversions found in one shot.
implementation.explain: The naive count is a double loop at O(n^2). What makes the merge version work is that the merge already knows an ordering fact the double loop would have to rediscover: when R[j] jumps ahead of the whole remaining left half, that is |L| - i inversions counted in constant time rather than one at a time. Use `<=` on the tie or equal values get counted as inversions.

implementation.prompt: This `merge` is wrong. `merge([1,3,5], [2,4,6])` should give `[1,2,3,4,5,6]` but gives `[1,2,3,4,5]`. Find and fix the fault.
implementation.hint: The main loop stops as soon as either side is exhausted. Both sides need draining, not just one.
implementation.explain: Only one drain loop is present, so whenever `b` outlives `a` its tail is silently dropped. The `[9], [1,2,3]` case is the giveaway: the bug is invisible whenever the largest element happens to live in `a`, which is exactly why one hand-picked example is not a test suite.

implementation.prompt: Write `quickSortMedian3(a)` - quicksort that chooses its pivot as the **median of the first, middle and last** element of each range (`mid = Math.floor((lo + hi) / 2)`), swaps it to the end, then Lomuto-partitions as usual. Return a new sorted array; do not call the built-in `sort`.
implementation.hint: Sorting three [value, index] pairs and taking the middle one's index is the least fiddly way to get the median index.
implementation.explain: The already-sorted ten-element test is the whole point: a last-element pivot would spend 45 comparisons there and grow quadratically, while median-of-three picks the true middle and splits evenly. The three extra comparisons per call are O(1) and disappear into the constant factor.

implementation.prompt: Quicksort takes the last element of every range as its pivot. Give its worst-case running time on $n$ elements, name an input that achieves it, and derive the bound from the recurrence that input produces.
implementation.explain: Already-sorted input makes the last element the maximum every time, so each split is n-1 and 0 rather than two halves. That gives T(n) = T(n-1) + Theta(n), and summing n + (n-1) + ... + 1 gives n(n-1)/2 comparisons - quadratic. The average case is still Theta(n log n) because most pivots split at least somewhat evenly, but an average is not a guarantee.

implementation.prompt: Trace Lomuto partition on `[7, 2, 9, 4, 3, 8, 5]` with `lo = 0`, `hi = 6`, pivot `a[hi] = 5` and boundary `i` starting at 0. The loop runs `j` from 0 to 5, and when `a[j] < pivot` it swaps `a[i]` with `a[j]` then increments `i`. Give the whole array after each `j` iteration (written as `[1,2,3]`), then after the final pivot swap, then the index returned.
implementation.explain: Notice the left region [2,4,3] is not sorted and never becomes sorted here - partition promises only that everything before index 3 is below 5 and everything after is above it. Notice too that j = 0, 2 and 5 change nothing: a scan step with no swap still costs a comparison, which is why the cost is hi - lo regardless of the data.

implementation.prompt: This quicksort returns `[2,1]` for `[2,1]` and leaves `[5,4,3,2,1]` completely untouched, yet it never crashes or hangs. One line is missing. Restore it.
implementation.hint: After the sweep, index i is the boundary the pivot belongs on - but the pivot is still sitting at hi.
implementation.explain: Without the final swap the pivot never moves off `hi`, so the recursion on `lo..i-1` and `i+1..hi` is arranging elements around a boundary cell that holds the wrong value. It still terminates, because the ranges do shrink correctly, which is why the failure is silent wrong output rather than a crash - the most expensive kind of bug.

implementation.prompt: Quicksort is quoted as $O(n \log n)$ **expected** rather than simply $O(n \log n)$. Explain what the word expected is doing there, and why choosing the pivot more cleverly cannot remove the $\Theta(n^2)$ worst case for any fixed deterministic rule.
implementation.explain: Expected is an average - over inputs, or over the random choices of a randomised pivot - not a bound on every run. For any fixed deterministic rule an adversary can read the rule and construct the input that always hands it an extreme element, so the quadratic case survives. Randomising the pivot does not delete that case either; it only makes it impossible for an adversary to aim at it.

level-project.prompt:
Build a comparison-counting benchmark harness.

Write `benchmark(sortFn, inputs)`. `sortFn(array, compare)` is any sort that makes all of its ordering decisions through the `compare` callback it is handed. `inputs` is an array of arrays of numbers.

For each input array, in order:

- pass `sortFn` a **copy** of the array - the caller's arrays must not be modified - together with a fresh `compare(x, y)` that counts every call and returns `x - y`;
- record how many times `compare` was called during that run;
- check whether the array `sortFn` returned really is ascending, **without** using the counting comparator, so that your own check cannot inflate the count.

Return `{ runs, totalComparisons, maxComparisons }`, where `runs` is an array of `{ n, comparisons, sorted }` - one per input, in input order, with `n` the input length and `sorted` a boolean. `totalComparisons` sums every run and `maxComparisons` is the largest single run; both are `0` when `inputs` is empty.

tests.input: (function (a, cmp) { for (let i = 0; i < a.length; i++) for (let j = 0; j < a.length - 1 - i; j++) if (cmp(a[j], a[j + 1]) > 0) { const t = a[j]; a[j] = a[j + 1]; a[j + 1] = t; } return a; }), [[3, 1, 2]]
(function (a, cmp) { for (let i = 0; i < a.length; i++) for (let j = 0; j < a.length - 1 - i; j++) if (cmp(a[j], a[j + 1]) > 0) { const t = a[j]; a[j] = a[j + 1]; a[j + 1] = t; } return a; }), []

(function (a, cmp) { for (let i = 0; i < a.length; i++) for (let j = 0; j < a.length - 1 - i; j++) if (cmp(a[j], a[j + 1]) > 0) { const t = a[j]; a[j] = a[j + 1]; a[j + 1] = t; } return a; }), [[], [1]]

(function (a, cmp) { for (let i = 0; i < a.length; i++) for (let j = 0; j < a.length - 1 - i; j++) if (cmp(a[j], a[j + 1]) > 0) { const t = a[j]; a[j] = a[j + 1]; a[j + 1] = t; } return a; }), [[4, 3, 2, 1], [1, 2]]
(function (a, cmp) { if (a.length > 1) cmp(a[0], a[1]); return a; }), [[2, 1]]

level-project.hint: Declare `comparisons` fresh inside the loop, before you build `compare`, so each run closes over its own counter. `input.slice()` is the copy.
level-project.explain: Counting comparisons rather than timing is what makes a sorting benchmark reproducible: wall-clock time depends on the machine, the JIT and cache behaviour, but the comparison count is a property of the algorithm and the input alone. The empty-`inputs` case matters because a maximum over nothing has no natural value - you must choose 0 rather than let -Infinity or undefined leak out. And verifying sortedness outside the counted comparator is the discipline that stops a measuring instrument from perturbing what it measures.

exam.prompt: What does this print? The counter is reset between the two merges.
exam.explain: Each comparison emits exactly one element and the loop stops the moment either side empties, so merging p and q elements costs between min(p,q) and p+q-1 comparisons - never more. Here both cases exhaust one side after three emissions and the drain loops finish the rest for free.

exam.prompt: Give the **auxiliary space** merge sort needs on an array of $n$ elements, beyond the input itself, and justify it. Account for both the merge buffers and the recursion stack.
exam.explain: A merge cannot safely write over its own inputs, so it needs a buffer, and the outermost merge alone handles all n elements - Theta(n). The recursion stack is only Theta(log n) frames deep, so it is dominated. This is exactly the trade quicksort refuses to make: it partitions in place and spends only stack, which is why it wins when memory is the binding constraint.

exam.prompt: Write `mergeSortBy(a, keyFn)` returning a new array holding `a`'s elements sorted ascending by `keyFn(element)`, and **stable** - equal keys keep their original relative order. Use merge sort; do not call the built-in `sort`. Keys may be numbers or strings.
exam.hint: Split before you compare anything, and let `<=` on the keys award ties to the left half - which is the earlier half of the original array.
exam.explain: Stability comes for free here only because the left half is always the earlier part of the original array and `<=` gives it the tie. That is a property of the split-and-merge structure; quicksort has no such invariant, since partitioning swaps elements across arbitrary distances and destroys the original relative order of equals.

exam.prompt: `mergeSort([5, 2, 4, 1])` splits at `mid = 2`, recurses on the left half before the right, and merges on the way back up. Give each merge's result in the order the merges complete, then how many merge calls happen in total. Write arrays as `[1,2,3]`.
exam.explain: Three merges for four elements is no coincidence: every merge collapses two subarrays into one, so sorting n elements takes exactly n-1 merges, spread over log2(n) levels. Counting them is a cheap sanity check on any merge sort you write.

exam.prompt: Complete Lomuto partition. In order the blanks are: the index the pivot is read from, the comparison that stops the sweep one short of the pivot, the operator that advances the boundary, and the index the pivot is finally swapped with.
exam.explain: `j < hi` rather than `j <= hi` keeps the pivot out of its own sweep - include it and the pivot could be swapped away from the end, leaving the final swap to move the wrong element. The boundary `i` only advances on a swap, which is what keeps `a[lo..i-1]` exactly the known-smaller region.

exam.prompt: You must sort 50 million records on a machine with barely enough memory to hold them, and separately sort a few thousand integers inside a tight inner loop. Argue which of merge sort and quicksort fits each job, naming the property that decides it.
exam.explain: The deciding properties are space and guarantees, not the n log n they share. Quicksort sorts in place with a small constant factor and good locality, so it wins the tight inner loop where an O(n) buffer would be waste; merge sort's O(n) buffer is what buys the guaranteed worst case and stability, and it is also the only one of the two that survives data too large for memory, because merging is inherently sequential.

exam.prompt: A quicksort always takes the **last** element of a range as its pivot. Which input drives it to its $\Theta(n^2)$ worst case?
choices: An array already sorted in ascending order
An array whose elements alternate between high and low values
An array in which the median happens to sit last
An array of distinct values in a randomly chosen order
exam.explain: Ascending input makes the last element the maximum of every range, so each partition splits into n-1 and 0 and the recursion depth becomes n instead of log n. A median pivot is the best possible case and random order gives the n log n average - the pathological input here is the one that looks most benign.

exam.prompt: Write `medianOfThree(a, lo, hi)` returning the **index** of the median of the three values `a[lo]`, `a[mid]` and `a[hi]`, where `mid = Math.floor((lo + hi) / 2)`. Return one of `lo`, `mid` or `hi`. When those three indices coincide, return that index.
exam.hint: Pair each value with its index, order the three pairs, and read the index out of the middle one - far less error-prone than nested if-statements.
exam.explain: It must return an index, not a value, because the caller swaps that element to the end before partitioning and a value alone would not say which cell to swap. The `[5], 0, 0` case is the degenerate range quicksort meets at the bottom of the recursion, and solutions built from nested comparisons of three supposedly distinct positions usually break there.

exam.prompt: Put one call to quicksort on the range `lo..hi` in the order its steps execute.
fragments: Recursively quicksort the part to the right of the pivot
Choose a pivot element from the range
Return immediately if the range holds fewer than two elements
Partition the range so smaller elements sit left of the pivot and larger ones right
Recursively quicksort the part to the left of the pivot
exam.explain: All the work happens at the top, before the recursion - the opposite of merge sort, where the recursion comes first and the work is on the way back up. That is why quicksort needs no combine step at all: once partition returns, the pivot is already final and the two sides are wholly independent.

exam.prompt: Give the **expected** running time of quicksort with a well-chosen pivot on $n$ elements, derive it from the recurrence a balanced split produces, and say in one line why this is not the same claim as merge sort's bound.
exam.explain: A balanced split gives T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Theta(n) - the same recurrence as merge sort, hence the same Theta(n log n). The difference is that merge sort's split is guaranteed by construction while quicksort's depends on the pivot landing near the median, so quicksort's bound holds on average and its worst case is still Theta(n^2). Even a split as lopsided as 9:1 stays Theta(n log n), since it only changes the depth by a constant factor.

lesson.title: Trees, Order, and the Cost of Shape

sections.title: A Node Is a Plain Object
sections.body:
A **binary tree** needs no class: a node is an object with a `value` and two links, `left` and `right`, each holding either another node or `null`. The single node nothing points at is the **root**; a node whose links are both `null` is a **leaf**.

Because `left` and `right` are themselves trees - possibly empty ones - almost every tree function is recursive with `null` as its base case. `countNodes` below asks each subtree for its own count and adds one for itself.

Nothing here enforces order yet. This is only the shape: values, links, and a `null` that means *no subtree*.

annotations.text: Just an object literal. No class, no library - a tree is a value like any other.
A leaf is defined by its links, not by its depth: both children absent.
`null` is the base case. Every recursive tree function needs one, or it walks off the edge.
One for this node, plus whatever the two subtrees report. This is $O(n)$: each node is visited once.

checkpoint.prompt: Write `countLeaves(root)` returning how many leaves the tree holds - nodes whose `left` and `right` are both `null`. The empty tree has 0 leaves.

tests.input: { value: 8, left: { value: 3, left: { value: 1, left: null, right: null }, right: { value: 6, left: null, right: null } }, right: { value: 10, left: null, right: null } }

checkpoint.explain: Two base cases carry the whole function: `null` contributes nothing and a leaf contributes exactly one. The recursive case never counts itself, which is why an internal node with a single child still reports only what its subtrees found.
checkpoint.hint: Check `root === null` first, then the both-children-null case, then recurse on each side.

sections.title: The Ordering Invariant
sections.body:
A **binary search tree** adds one rule to that shape: for every node, every value in its left subtree is smaller than the node's value, and every value in its right subtree is larger. This is the **BST invariant**, and it constrains whole subtrees, not just immediate children.

The invariant turns a search into a sequence of decisions. `contains` compares once per node and then discards an entire subtree, never looking at it again - it cannot backtrack, it can only descend.

`insert` is the same descent, and the place it falls off the tree into `null` is exactly where the new node belongs. Both functions do work proportional to the **depth they reach**, not to the number of nodes.

annotations.text: Falling off the tree into `null` is the answer: this empty spot is where the value belongs.
Smaller goes left. Reassigning the link is what stitches the returned subtree back on.
Equal values fall through to `return root` unchanged, so this tree holds a set.
One comparison eliminates the entire other subtree. That is the whole gain.
Inserted in the order 8, 3, 10, 1, 6, 14: root 8, then 3 and 10 as its children.

checkpoint.prompt: Write `smallest(root)` returning the smallest value in a BST, using the invariant rather than scanning every node. Return `null` for the empty tree.

tests.input: { value: 8, left: { value: 3, left: { value: 1, left: null, right: null }, right: { value: 6, left: null, right: null } }, right: { value: 10, left: null, right: null } }

checkpoint.explain: Every left step moves into a subtree whose values are all smaller than everything above it, so the first node with no left child has nothing smaller anywhere in the tree. No right link is ever followed, which is why this costs the height rather than the node count.
checkpoint.hint: A loop that keeps doing `cur = cur.left` until `cur.left` is null.

sections.title: Three Walks, One Shape
sections.body:
A **traversal** visits every node once; the three classic orders differ only in *when* a node records itself relative to its two recursive calls. **Pre-order** records before descending, **in-order** records between the two descents, and **post-order** records after both.

On a BST, in-order is special. The recursion emits everything smaller than the node, then the node, then everything larger - and by the invariant that is exactly ascending order, at every node, all the way down.

So an in-order walk of a BST is a sorted listing, and it costs $O(n)$ because each node is pushed exactly once. Pre-order and post-order visit the same nodes for the same cost but offer no such guarantee.

annotations.text: Pre-order: record, then left, then right. The root always comes out first.
In-order: the push sits between the two calls. That single placement is what sorts the output.
Post-order: both children are finished before the node is recorded, so the root comes out last.
Sorted, from a tree nobody ever sorted. The invariant did the work at insert time.

checkpoint.prompt: Write `sortedValues(root)` returning an array of every value in the BST in ascending order, by walking it in-order. Do not call `.sort()`. The empty tree gives `[]`.

tests.input: { value: 8, left: { value: 3, left: { value: 1, left: null, right: null }, right: { value: 6, left: null, right: null } }, right: { value: 10, left: null, right: { value: 14, left: null, right: null } } }

checkpoint.explain: The output comes back sorted without a single comparison being made during the walk - the ordering was paid for when the tree was built, and the traversal only reads it back. Move the `push` above `walk(n.left)` and the same tree yields pre-order instead.
checkpoint.hint: An inner `walk(n)` that returns on null, recurses left, pushes, then recurses right.

sections.title: Height Is the Real Cost
sections.body:
Define **height** as the number of edges on the longest root-to-leaf path: a single node has height $0$ and the empty tree has height $-1$. Search and insert cost $O(h)$, not $O(n)$ - the node count only bounds how good $h$ could possibly be.

A tree of $n$ nodes can be as short as $h = \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$, which is why a balanced BST searches in $O(\log n)$. But nothing in `insert` enforces balance.

Feed it already-sorted input and every value goes right, producing a chain of $n$ nodes with $h = n - 1$. The BST has degenerated into a linked list: same code, same invariant, catastrophically different shape, and search is back to $O(n)$.

annotations.text: Edge count, so the empty tree is -1 and a lone node is 0. State the convention or the numbers mean nothing.
The same seven values, two insertion orders.
2 against 6: both trees hold seven nodes, one is three times taller.
The sorted build has no left child anywhere - a right-leaning chain, not a tree.

checkpoint.prompt: Write `height(root)` returning the number of edges on the longest root-to-leaf path. The empty tree is `-1` and a single node is `0`.

tests.input: { value: 1, left: null, right: { value: 2, left: null, right: { value: 3, left: null, right: null } } }
{ value: 4, left: { value: 2, left: null, right: null }, right: { value: 6, left: null, right: null } }

checkpoint.explain: The `-1` for the empty tree is what makes `1 + Math.max(...)` come out as `0` for a leaf, so the convention is not decoration - it is the arithmetic. The third tree and the fourth hold three nodes each and differ in height, which is exactly the gap between $O(n)$ and $O(\log n)$ behaviour.
checkpoint.hint: One base case returning -1, then `1 + Math.max(height(root.left), height(root.right))`.

guided-practice.prompt: What does this print?
guided-practice.explain: Reading a tree is nothing but following named properties, and `null` is a real value you can print and compare - it is the marker for *no subtree*, not an error. Note that `t.left.left` prints `null` while `t.left.left.value` would throw, which is why every recursive tree function tests for `null` before touching `.value`.

guided-practice.prompt: Fill the blanks so `contains` searches a BST by descending, never scanning both sides.
guided-practice.explain: The comparison is the whole algorithm: `<` sends the search into the subtree that, by the invariant, is the only place the value could be. Reverse it and the function still terminates and still returns a boolean - it just answers `false` for values that are present, which is far worse than crashing.

guided-practice.prompt: Write `largest(root)` returning the largest value in a BST, or `null` for the empty tree. Use the invariant - do not visit every node.

tests.input: { value: 8, left: { value: 3, left: null, right: null }, right: { value: 10, left: null, right: { value: 14, left: null, right: null } } }
{ value: 9, left: { value: 2, left: null, right: { value: 4, left: null, right: null } }, right: null }

guided-practice.explain: The last test is the one that matters: a node with a left subtree and no right child is itself the maximum, so the loop must stop on a missing right link rather than assume it has reached a leaf. The cost is the length of the rightmost path, which is at most the height.
guided-practice.hint: Walk right while `cur.right !== null`, then return `cur.value`.

guided-practice.prompt: What does this print?
guided-practice.explain: Both duplicate inserts fall through to the final `return root` without building anything, because the value is neither `<` nor `>` the node it lands on. That silent no-op is a design decision, not a bug: this BST stores a set, and storing multiplicity would mean adding a count field to the node.

guided-practice.prompt: The values `[8, 3, 10, 1, 6, 14]` are inserted in that order into an empty BST. Give the values in the order a **pre-order** traversal emits them, one per step.
guided-practice.explain: Pre-order records a node before descending, so the sequence is a depth-first plunge: the whole left subtree is drained before the right one is entered at all. Because the root leads, replaying a pre-order listing through `insert` rebuilds this exact tree - replaying the in-order listing would not, since sorted input always builds a chain.

guided-practice.prompt: Write `contains(root, value)` returning `true` if the BST holds that value and `false` otherwise. Descend using the invariant; never look at both subtrees of a node.

tests.input: { value: 8, left: { value: 3, left: { value: 1, left: null, right: null }, right: { value: 6, left: null, right: null } }, right: { value: 10, left: null, right: null } }, 6
{ value: 8, left: { value: 3, left: { value: 1, left: null, right: null }, right: { value: 6, left: null, right: null } }, right: { value: 10, left: null, right: null } }, 7

guided-practice.explain: The absent-value test is the important one: the search for 7 stops when it falls off the tree at a `null`, having compared against only 8, 3 and 6. A failed search costs the same as a successful one at the same depth, so the worst case for both is the height of the tree.
guided-practice.hint: Three cases in order: null, equal, then one recursive call chosen by `<`.

guided-practice.prompt: Order these fragments into a function that appends a node's value **in-order** into `out`.
guided-practice.explain: Only one line moves between the three traversal orders - the `push`. Lifting it above the left recursion gives pre-order and dropping it below the right recursion gives post-order, out of the same four lines of control flow.

implementation.prompt: Write `insert(root, value)` returning the root of the BST after adding `value`. Inserting into `null` returns a new node `{ value, left: null, right: null }`; a value already present must leave the tree unchanged.

tests.input: { value: 5, left: { value: 3, left: null, right: null }, right: null }, 3

implementation.explain: Returning the root on every path is what makes the reattachment `root.left = insert(root.left, value)` work uniformly: the recursive call hands back either the unchanged subtree or a brand-new node, and the caller never needs to know which. Drop the final `return root` and every node above the insertion point is lost.
implementation.hint: Four branches - null, less, greater, equal - and a single `return root` at the end.

implementation.prompt: `build([5, 2, 8, 1])` should return `[1, 2, 5, 8]` but returns `[8, 5, 2, 1]`. One pair of comparisons in `insert` sends values to the wrong subtree. Fix `insert` without changing `build` or `inOrder`.
implementation.explain: A mirrored insert still builds a perfectly valid binary tree that never crashes - it just satisfies the reversed invariant, so the in-order walk reads it back descending. This is the failure mode to fear in tree code: the structure is intact and only the ordering contract is broken, so nothing throws and the bug surfaces as quietly wrong output.
implementation.hint: Smaller values belong on the left. Swap the two subtree names in the comparisons.

implementation.prompt: Write `traverse(root, order)` where `order` is the string `"pre"`, `"in"` or `"post"`, returning the array of values in that traversal order. The empty tree gives `[]` for every order.

tests.input: { value: 8, left: { value: 3, left: { value: 1, left: null, right: null }, right: { value: 6, left: null, right: null } }, right: { value: 10, left: null, right: { value: 14, left: null, right: null } } }, "pre"

{ value: 8, left: { value: 3, left: { value: 1, left: null, right: null }, right: { value: 6, left: null, right: null } }, right: { value: 10, left: null, right: { value: 14, left: null, right: null } } }, "in"

{ value: 8, left: { value: 3, left: { value: 1, left: null, right: null }, right: { value: 6, left: null, right: null } }, right: { value: 10, left: null, right: { value: 14, left: null, right: null } } }, "post"

implementation.explain: Writing all three in one walker makes the real claim visible: the recursion is identical and only the position of the visit changes. All three cost $O(n)$ time and $O(h)$ extra space for the call stack, so the choice between them is never about cost - it is about what the order guarantees. Only `"in"` comes back sorted, and only on a BST.
implementation.hint: One inner `walk(n)` with three guarded pushes: before the left call, between the calls, after the right call.

implementation.prompt: Write `bstSort(values)` which inserts every number of `values` into an initially empty BST and returns the in-order walk of the result. Duplicates are dropped. Do not call `.sort()`.
implementation.explain: This is a genuine sorting algorithm, and all of its cost is in the building phase: the walk is always $O(n)$, but the $n$ inserts total $O(n \log n)$ only if the tree stays short. The already-sorted test case is the worst input, not the easiest - it builds a chain, so the inserts degrade to $\Theta(n^2)$, which is why nobody ships an unbalanced BST as a sorter.
implementation.hint: Reuse `insert` from earlier, then an in-order walk pushing into an array.

implementation.prompt: Write `shape(root)` returning the array `[nodeCount, height]`, where height is the number of edges on the longest root-to-leaf path and the empty tree gives `[0, -1]`.

tests.input: { value: 1, left: null, right: { value: 2, left: null, right: { value: 3, left: null, right: null } } }
{ value: 2, left: { value: 1, left: null, right: null }, right: { value: 3, left: null, right: null } }

{ value: 4, left: { value: 2, left: { value: 1, left: null, right: null }, right: { value: 3, left: null, right: null } }, right: { value: 6, left: { value: 5, left: null, right: null }, right: { value: 7, left: null, right: null } } }

implementation.explain: The third and fourth trees hold the same three nodes and differ in height, which is the entire point: $n$ constrains $h$ only from below, by $h \ge \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$, and never from above. The last case shows the best possible shape for seven nodes - height 2, since $2^3 - 1 = 7$.
implementation.hint: One recursive call per side, then combine: counts add, heights take the max plus one.

implementation.prompt: Write `isBST(root)` returning `true` only if the whole tree satisfies the BST invariant - every value in a node's left subtree strictly smaller than it, every value on the right strictly larger. Checking only immediate children is not enough. The empty tree is `true`.

tests.input: { value: 8, left: { value: 3, left: { value: 1, left: null, right: null }, right: { value: 6, left: null, right: null } }, right: { value: 10, left: null, right: null } }
{ value: 8, left: { value: 3, left: null, right: { value: 9, left: null, right: null } }, right: { value: 10, left: null, right: null } }
{ value: 5, left: { value: 5, left: null, right: null }, right: null }

implementation.explain: The fourth test is the trap: 9 is correctly to the right of 3, so a check that only compares parents with their children says yes - but 9 sits in the left subtree of 8 while being larger than 8, so a search for 9 would descend right and never find it. The invariant is a claim about subtrees, so the check must carry a range downwards, tightening one bound at every step.
implementation.hint: `ok(n, low, high)` returning true for null, recursing with `ok(n.left, low, n.value)` and `ok(n.right, n.value, high)`.

analysis.prompt: A BST holds $n$ nodes and is perfectly balanced. Give the worst-case time of `contains(root, value)` as a function of $n$, and justify it in terms of what a single comparison buys you.
analysis.explain: The honest statement of the cost is $O(h)$ - the search does constant work per level and can only descend. Balance is what converts that into $O(\log n)$: each comparison discards one subtree, in a balanced tree that subtree holds about half the remaining nodes, so the candidate set halves every step and reaches one after $\log_2 n$ steps.

analysis.prompt: The values $1, 2, 3, \ldots, n$ are inserted in ascending order into an empty BST using the lesson's `insert`. Give the worst-case time of a single `contains` call on the resulting tree, and describe the shape that causes it.
analysis.explain: Every value is larger than everything already in the tree, so every insert walks the full right spine and attaches at the bottom: no node ever acquires a left child. The result has $h = n - 1$, so it is a linked list wearing tree syntax, and the $O(h)$ bound - which was never a lie - now evaluates to $O(n)$. The invariant still holds perfectly; it is the shape, not the ordering, that failed.

analysis.prompt: Give the total time to **build** the tree in the previous question - all $n$ ascending inserts into an initially empty BST - and justify the total by summing the cost of the individual inserts.
analysis.explain: The $i$-th insert walks past the $i-1$ nodes already in the chain, so the total is $0 + 1 + \cdots + (n-1) = n(n-1)/2$, which is $\Theta(n^2)$. This is why `bstSort` is quadratic on sorted input and $O(n \log n)$ on well-mixed input: the algorithm never changed, only the shape its input produced. Reading the answer back out is $O(n)$ either way.

analysis.prompt: The values `[5, 2, 8, 1, 3, 9]` are inserted in that order into an empty BST. Give the values in the order a **post-order** traversal emits them.
analysis.explain: Post-order finishes both children before recording a node, so a parent can never appear before any of its descendants and the root is always last. That property is what makes post-order the order for anything that must consume its children first - freeing a tree, computing subtree sizes, or evaluating an expression tree bottom-up.

analysis.prompt: In-order traversal of a BST emits values in ascending order, but pre-order on the same tree does not. Explain what the in-order placement of the visit guarantees at every node that the pre-order placement does not.
analysis.explain: In-order emits (everything left) then (this node) then (everything right), and the invariant says the left block lies entirely below the node and the right block entirely above it - so the node lands exactly between two blocks that are, by induction, already sorted. Pre-order emits the node first, ahead of a left subtree that is entirely smaller than it, so the very first pair of values is already out of order unless the root has no left child at all.

analysis.prompt: Prove that in-order traversal of a binary search tree outputs its values in strictly ascending order. Use induction on the height of the tree, and state clearly which case is the base case and where the BST invariant is used.
analysis.explain: The proof is short because the invariant does the work. Base case: the empty tree emits nothing, which is vacuously ascending. Inductive step: for a node $v$ at height $h$, both subtrees have height less than $h$, so by hypothesis in-order emits each as an ascending sequence; the invariant says every value on the left is $< v$ and every value on the right is $> v$; therefore the concatenation (left, $v$, right) is ascending. The induction runs on height rather than node count because height is what strictly decreases when you step into a subtree.

exam.prompt: Which statement is the BST invariant?
choices: A node's left child is smaller than it and its right child is larger
Every value in a node's left subtree is smaller than the node, and every value in its right subtree is larger
Every leaf sits at the same depth, so the tree is balanced
The values appear in ascending order when each level is read left to right
exam.explain: The first choice is the invariant weakened to immediate children, and that weaker rule is not enough: a value can be correctly placed relative to its parent and still sit in the wrong subtree three levels up, where a search will never look for it. Balance is a separate property the invariant says nothing about.

exam.prompt: What does this print?
exam.explain: Two trees with identical in-order output and wildly different heights - proof that the in-order listing does not determine the shape. That is exactly why a sorted array cannot simply be replayed through `insert` to rebuild a short tree: the ordering survives the round trip, the structure does not.

exam.prompt: Fill the blanks so `height` returns the number of edges on the longest root-to-leaf path, with `-1` for the empty tree.
exam.explain: The `-1` is forced by the arithmetic, not by taste: a leaf must come out as 0, and `1 + max(-1, -1)` is the only way to get there. Return 0 for the empty tree instead and you have silently switched to counting nodes on the path rather than edges - a legitimate convention, but every stated bound then shifts by one.

exam.prompt: A BST was built by inserting `[8, 3, 10, 1, 6, 14]` in that order. Trace `contains(root, 7)`: give the value at each node it compares against, then what the next call receives, then what it returns.

steps.label: what the 4th recursive call receives as root

exam.explain: The search compares three of the six nodes and then falls off the tree, which is the whole economy of a BST: an unsuccessful search costs the depth of where the value *would* have gone, not a scan. The `null` it lands on is exactly the spot `insert(root, 7)` would fill - search and insert follow the identical path.

exam.prompt: Write `depthOf(root, value)` returning the number of edges from the root to the node holding `value`, or `-1` if the value is absent. The root itself is at depth `0`. Search using the invariant.

tests.input: { value: 8, left: { value: 3, left: { value: 1, left: null, right: null }, right: { value: 6, left: null, right: null } }, right: { value: 10, left: null, right: null } }, 6
{ value: 8, left: { value: 3, left: { value: 1, left: null, right: null }, right: { value: 6, left: null, right: null } }, right: { value: 10, left: null, right: null } }, 10
{ value: 8, left: { value: 3, left: { value: 1, left: null, right: null }, right: { value: 6, left: null, right: null } }, right: { value: 10, left: null, right: null } }, 7

exam.explain: The depth a value sits at *is* the cost of finding it, so this function measures the very quantity every complexity claim on this floor is about. Writing it as a loop rather than a recursion is possible only because the search never backtracks - there is no work left to do on the way back up, which is not true of a search through a general binary tree.
exam.hint: A `while (cur !== null)` loop that increments a counter each time it steps down.

exam.prompt: Give the worst-case time of an in-order traversal that collects all $n$ values of a BST into an array, and say why the tree's shape does not change that answer even though it changes the cost of `contains`.
exam.explain: A traversal has no decisions to make: it visits every node exactly once and does constant work there, so it is $\Theta(n)$ on any shape. Search is different precisely because it *skips* - its cost is the length of the path it takes, so shape governs it. The one thing shape still controls here is the recursion stack, which is $O(h)$ and so degrades from $O(\log n)$ to $O(n)$ on a chain.

exam.prompt: A service keeps a BST of user ids and reimports its nightly backup, which is written out sorted by id. Lookups that used to be instant now take milliseconds each, though the code and the data are unchanged. Explain what the import did to the tree and why the invariant being intact does not save it.
exam.explain: Inserting in sorted order sends every value down the right spine, so the rebuilt tree is a chain of height $n-1$ and lookups became linear. The invariant is still perfectly satisfied, and that is the uncomfortable part: correctness is untouched and only cost collapsed, so no test that checks answers will ever catch it. The fixes are to shuffle the input, insert from the middle outwards, or use a tree that rebalances itself.

exam.prompt: Write `valuesInRange(root, low, high)` returning, in ascending order, every value `v` in the BST with `low <= v && v <= high`. Use the invariant to skip subtrees that cannot contain any answer - do not walk the whole tree and filter.

tests.input: { value: 8, left: { value: 3, left: { value: 1, left: null, right: null }, right: { value: 6, left: null, right: null } }, right: { value: 10, left: null, right: { value: 14, left: null, right: null } } }, 3, 10

{ value: 8, left: { value: 3, left: { value: 1, left: null, right: null }, right: { value: 6, left: null, right: null } }, right: { value: 10, left: null, right: { value: 14, left: null, right: null } } }, 0, 20

{ value: 8, left: { value: 3, left: { value: 1, left: null, right: null }, right: { value: 6, left: null, right: null } }, right: { value: 10, left: null, right: { value: 14, left: null, right: null } } }, 7, 7

exam.explain: The two guards are pure invariant reasoning: if `n.value <= low` then the entire left subtree lies below `low`, so there is nothing there worth visiting. That prunes the walk to $O(h + k)$ for $k$ results instead of $O(n)$, and it is the same pruning that makes a BST worth building in the first place. The result is already ascending because the skeleton is still an in-order walk.
exam.hint: In-order walk with `if (low < n.value)` guarding the left call and `if (n.value < high)` guarding the right one.

exam.prompt: `sizeOf` should return the number of nodes but throws `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded` on every non-empty tree. Fix it; `sizeOf(null)` must return `0`.

tests.input: { value: 8, left: { value: 3, left: null, right: null }, right: null }
{ value: 8, left: { value: 3, left: { value: 1, left: null, right: null }, right: { value: 6, left: null, right: null } }, right: { value: 10, left: null, right: null } }

exam.explain: The base case tests for the wrong absent-value: the tree marks a missing child with `null`, and `null === undefined` is `false` under strict equality, so the guard never fires and the recursion runs off the bottom of the tree. A base case that cannot match is not a base case, and on a recursive structure the symptom is always the stack, never a wrong number.
exam.hint: What value do a leaf's `left` and `right` actually hold?

exam.prompt: A BST is built by inserting `[6, 4, 9, 2, 5, 8]` in that order. Order these values as a **post-order** traversal emits them.
exam.explain: Work bottom-up: the left subtree rooted at 4 finishes first and emits 2, 5, 4; the right subtree rooted at 9 emits 8 then 9, since 8 is its left child; and the root 6 can only be emitted once both are done. A post-order listing always ends at the root, which is how you recognise one at a glance.

exam.prompt: You must store $n$ keys in a BST and support lookup. Give the worst-case lookup cost of a tree built by inserting the keys already sorted, and contrast the height that build produces with the height expected from a random insertion order.
exam.explain: Sorted input yields a chain with $h = n-1$ and therefore $O(n)$ lookups; a random insertion order gives an expected height of $\Theta(\log n)$ and so $O(\log n)$ expected lookups. The difference lies entirely in the insertion order, not in the data, which is why real systems either randomise that order or use a structure that rebalances rather than trusting the input to arrive shuffled.

lesson.title: Vertices, Edges, and Two Ways to Walk Them

sections.title: A Graph Is a Map From Names to Neighbours
sections.body:
A **graph** is a set of vertices joined by edges, and the cheapest way to hold one in JavaScript is an **adjacency list**: a plain object whose keys are vertex names and whose values are arrays of neighbours.

An undirected edge appears **twice**, once in each endpoint's list, so summing every list length counts each edge twice and $E = \frac{1}{2}\sum_v \deg(v)$.

The cost model follows from the shape: asking *who is next to C* is one property lookup plus a walk of that one list, while asking *is A next to D* costs $O(\deg(A))$ because you must scan.

An adjacency list stores $V$ keys and $2E$ names, so it is $O(V + E)$ space, which is why it beats a $V \times V$ matrix on the sparse graphs you actually meet.

annotations.text: This graph is the Cistern. Every trace on this floor walks it, so learn its shape.
One key lookup, and the entire neighbour array is already in hand.
14 list entries, 7 edges: every undirected edge is stored at both of its ends.
A is not adjacent to D. Reaching D from A takes two edges, which is what BFS will tell us.

checkpoint.prompt: This adjacency list describes an undirected graph. What does the code print?
checkpoint.explain: Vertices are keys, so `Object.keys` counts $V$. Degrees sum to $2E$ in an undirected graph, so halving recovers the edge count without ever materialising an edge list. Adjacency is a membership test inside one array, and W's array holds only E.

sections.title: The Visited Set Is Not an Optimisation
sections.body:
Real graphs contain **cycles**, and a cycle means a walk can return to where it started. A traversal with no memory therefore never stops: it is not merely slow, it does not terminate.

The **visited set** is what makes traversal a finite algorithm. A vertex is marked the first time it is reached and skipped forever after.

That single rule is the termination argument. Every vertex is marked at most once, so the body of the loop runs at most $V$ times and each neighbour list is scanned at most once.

It also changes the answer, not just the runtime: without it a vertex is reported many times, once per distinct path that reaches it.

annotations.text: The budget is scaffolding, not part of the algorithm. It is the only reason this returns at all.
Prints A B A B C C A B C: A three times, B twice. Drop the budget and it recurses forever across the A-B edge.
One line, and the walk becomes finite: a marked vertex is never expanded again.

checkpoint.prompt: The graph `{ A: ["B"], B: ["A"] }` has one edge and no dead ends. Explain what a traversal with no visited set does on it, and why marking a vertex the first time it is reached makes the traversal stop.
checkpoint.explain: The A-B edge is a cycle of length two: expanding A reaches B, expanding B reaches A, forever. Termination is not a property of the graph, it is a property of the bookkeeping. Because each vertex is marked once and never expanded twice, the number of expansions is bounded above by $V$, which is finite.

sections.title: BFS: a Queue Buys You Shortest Paths
sections.body:
**Breadth-first search** keeps its frontier in a **queue**, so it removes vertices in the order they were discovered: first in, first out.

That one choice makes BFS visit the graph in layers, everything at distance 1 from the start, then everything at distance 2. Recording `dist[nb] = dist[node] + 1` at the moment of discovery therefore records the **fewest** edges, not merely some number of edges.

The reason is an invariant: the queue never holds vertices whose distances differ by more than one, and it holds them in non-decreasing order. So the first time a vertex is discovered it is discovered from a vertex one layer closer to the start, and a later, longer route is thrown away by the visited check.

This holds only when every edge costs the same. Give edges weights and the layer argument collapses, because a two-edge path can be cheaper than a one-edge path.

annotations.text: The start is marked before the loop, or a cycle would queue it a second time.
shift takes from the FRONT. Change this one call to pop and BFS becomes a depth-first walk with wrong distances.
Marking at discovery, not at removal, is what stops two different neighbours queueing the same vertex twice.
Set once and never revised: the first discovery is already the shortest.

checkpoint.prompt: Write `bfsDistances(graph, start)` returning an object mapping every vertex reachable from `start` to its distance from `start` in edges. Vertices that cannot be reached must not appear as keys.
checkpoint.explain: The `dist` object doubles as the visited set, since a key exists exactly when the vertex has been discovered, so C is never re-dated when D reaches it a layer later. The isolated vertex C in the third graph never enters the queue, which is why it is correctly absent rather than recorded with some sentinel distance.
checkpoint.hint1: A vertex is discovered once; `nb in dist` is your visited test.

sections.title: DFS, and Why Both Cost $O(V + E)$
sections.body:
**Depth-first search** swaps the queue for a **stack**, either explicit or the call stack via recursion. It follows one branch as far as it will go, then backtracks.

DFS answers *is there a path* just as well as BFS, but its paths are not shortest. On the Cistern it reaches F fifth, along the route A, B, D, C, E, F, where BFS reports F at distance 3.

Both cost $O(V + E)$, for the same reason. The visited set lets each vertex be expanded once, contributing $O(V)$; expanding a vertex scans its list once, and $\sum_v \deg(v) = 2E$, contributing $O(E)$. Neither term dominates in general, so you must write both: on a sparse graph $E$ is near $V$, on a dense one $E$ is $\Theta(V^2)$.

The real difference is **space**. BFS holds a whole layer, DFS holds one root-to-frontier path, and both are $O(V)$ in the worst case, but they are worst on different graphs.

annotations.text: One visited set is threaded through every call. A fresh set per call would recurse until the stack overflows.
The stack version must test visited on POP: the same vertex can be pushed by several neighbours before any of them is popped.
Pushing in list order means the LAST neighbour is explored first, which is why the two printed orders differ.

checkpoint.prompt: Both functions perform a correct depth-first traversal of the Cistern from A. What are the two lines this prints?
checkpoint.answer:
recursive: A B D C E F
stack: A C E F D B
checkpoint.explain: Recursion descends into the first neighbour first; an explicit stack pops the last vertex pushed, so it enters C before B. Both are valid depth-first orders, which is the point: *the* DFS order is a property of the neighbour ordering and the container, never of the graph alone.

guided-practice.prompt: The graph below is undirected. What does this print?
guided-practice.explain: Reading $V$, $E$ and a degree straight off an adjacency list is the reflex the rest of the floor depends on. The halving is not a trick: an undirected edge is physically stored twice, so the raw entry count is always $2E$.

guided-practice.prompt: Complete `addEdge` so that it records an undirected edge in an adjacency-list object, creating either endpoint's array if it does not exist yet.
guided-practice.explain: An undirected edge is two directed entries; writing only one half produces a graph that traverses correctly in one direction and silently loses paths in the other. The `||` guard is what lets you build a graph from an edge list without declaring the vertices first.

guided-practice.prompt: Write `edgeCount(graph)` returning the number of **undirected** edges in an adjacency list where every edge is stored at both endpoints. An empty graph has 0 edges.
guided-practice.explain: Counting stored entries and halving is $O(V + E)$ and needs no set of seen pairs. It is also a correctness check on your data: an odd total means some edge was recorded at only one endpoint, so the graph is malformed rather than merely small.
guided-practice.hint1: Sum every neighbour array's length, then divide by two.

guided-practice.prompt: Put the body of the BFS loop back in the order that makes distances correct. The loop header `while (queue.length > 0)` is already in place.
guided-practice.explain: Removing from the front before expanding is what makes the frontier a queue rather than a bag. Marking the neighbour visited *before* pushing it, in the same breath as setting its distance, is the step that keeps a vertex out of the queue twice and fixes its distance at its first discovery.

guided-practice.prompt: This is the Reliquary, a different graph from the Cistern. What does the depth-first walk print?
guided-practice.explain: DFS commits to P's first neighbour Q and only comes back for S after the entire Q branch, including U three levels down, is exhausted. That is why S, a direct neighbour of the start, is reported last, and why DFS order says nothing about distance.
guided-practice.answer: P Q T R U S

guided-practice.prompt: The Cistern contains the cycle A-B-D-C-A. Explain what the visited set does to that cycle during BFS from A, and why removing the set makes the traversal run forever rather than merely doing extra work.
guided-practice.explain: The distinction is the point: a visited set is usually described as an optimisation, but on any graph with a cycle it is a correctness and termination requirement. It converts an unbounded walk over a finite graph into a loop that runs at most $V$ times.

implementation.prompt: Write `bfsOrder(graph, start)` returning an array of vertices in breadth-first order from `start`. Expand each vertex's neighbours in the order they appear in its list. Vertices in other components must not appear.
implementation.explain: Marking on discovery rather than on removal is the load-bearing decision: with marking at removal the same vertex can sit in the queue twice and be emitted twice. Reachability, not membership in the object, decides what comes out, which is why the isolated C never appears.
implementation.hint2: Mark a neighbour visited at the moment you push it, not when you pop it.

implementation.prompt: Write `dfsOrder(graph, start)` returning an array of vertices in depth-first order from `start`, descending into each vertex's neighbours in list order. Recursion or an explicit stack are both fine, but the result must match a recursive descent.
implementation.explain: Recursion is the easier way to get list-order DFS because the call stack backtracks for you. An explicit stack would need its pushes reversed to produce the same sequence, since a stack pops the last thing pushed, and that asymmetry is the whole difference between the two implementations.
implementation.hint1: Return immediately if the vertex is already in the visited set.
implementation.hint2: One shared visited set for all calls, never a fresh one per call.

implementation.prompt: Write `shortestPathLength(graph, start, goal)` returning the number of edges on a shortest path between them: `0` when `start === goal`, and `-1` when `goal` is unreachable.
implementation.explain: Returning at the moment of discovery is safe precisely because BFS discovers in non-decreasing distance order, so no later route can be shorter. The `-1` case costs a full traversal of the start's component, which is the honest price of proving that no path exists.
implementation.hint1: Store a distance the moment a vertex is discovered, then never touch it again.
implementation.hint2: If the queue empties without meeting the goal, there is no path.

implementation.prompt: This is meant to be `shortestPathLength`, and on many graphs it even gives the right answer. On the Vault graph `{ A: ["X", "B"], X: ["A", "G"], B: ["A", "C"], C: ["B", "D"], D: ["C", "G"], G: ["X", "D"] }` it reports A to G as 4 when the answer is 2. Find the single wrong call and fix it.
implementation.explain: `pop` turns the frontier from a queue into a stack, so the search plunges down the long A-B-C-D branch and discovers G from D before X ever gets its turn. Since a vertex's distance is fixed at first discovery and never revised, one wrong container silently converts a shortest-path algorithm into an any-path algorithm.
implementation.hint1: Which end of the array does BFS remove from?

implementation.prompt: Write `connectedComponents(graph)` returning how many connected components an undirected adjacency list has. An empty graph has 0.
implementation.explain: One visited set shared across every restart is what makes this $O(V + E)$ overall rather than $O(V \cdot (V + E))$: each vertex is expanded in exactly one traversal, so the outer loop is free apart from its $V$ membership tests. The count of restarts is the count of components.
implementation.hint1: Loop over every vertex, but only launch a traversal from one that is still unvisited.
implementation.hint2: Do NOT reset the visited set between traversals.

implementation.prompt: Give the worst-case time complexity of BFS over an adjacency list in terms of $V$ and $E$. Justify both terms: say how many times a single vertex is expanded and why, how the neighbour scanning totals $2E$, and what the cost is on a graph of many vertices with no edges at all.
implementation.explain: The two terms come from two different accountings: the visited set caps expansions at $V$, and $\sum_v \deg(v) = 2E$ caps the total neighbour scanning at $O(E)$. Neither absorbs the other, because a graph with many isolated vertices has $E \ll V$ while a dense graph has $E = \Theta(V^2)$.

tracing.prompt: Run the BFS from the lesson on the Cistern `{ A: ["B", "C"], B: ["A", "D"], C: ["A", "D", "E"], D: ["B", "C", "F"], E: ["C", "F"], F: ["D", "E"] }` starting at A. After each iteration of the while loop (one shift plus all of that vertex's pushes), give the contents of the queue, front first, in the form `[C, D]`. Write `[]` for an empty queue.
tracing.explain: Watch the queue never hold two distances further apart than one: it is [1,1], then [1,2], then [2,2], then [2,3]. That monotone frontier is exactly the invariant that makes the first discovery of a vertex the shortest one, and it is what `pop` destroys.

tracing.prompt: Run the recursive DFS on the same Cistern from A, descending into neighbours in list order. Each time a vertex is marked visited, give the chain of active calls from A down to it, outermost first, in the form `A B D`.
tracing.explain: On this graph DFS never backtracks until every vertex is marked, so the call chain grows to depth 6, the whole of $V$. That is the worst-case $O(V)$ stack space of DFS made concrete, and the reason deep graphs blow a real call stack while BFS on the same graph holds only a two-vertex layer.

steps.label: when the 6th vertex is marked
steps.expected: A B D C E F

tracing.prompt: BFS from A on the Cistern builds a tree: the parent of a vertex is whichever vertex was being expanded when it was first discovered. Give the BFS parent of each vertex below. Then compare with the DFS parents from the previous trace.
tracing.explain: BFS and DFS agree on B and D here but disagree on C and F, and the disagreement is the whole story: BFS attaches F to D at depth 3, DFS attaches it to E at depth 5. Both are spanning trees of the same graph; only the BFS one has depth equal to distance.

tracing.prompt: BFS on the Cistern reports F at distance 3, and DFS reaches F only after A, B, D, C and E. Explain why swapping the queue for a stack loses the shortest-path guarantee, and say what has to be true of every edge's cost for the queue argument to work at all.
tracing.explain: A stack removes the most recently discovered vertex, so the search plunges instead of sweeping and the frontier no longer holds vertices in non-decreasing distance. The guarantee is also conditional on every edge having equal cost: with weights, a path of more edges can be cheaper, and the layer argument gives no information about cost.

exam.prompt: What does this breadth-first walk of the Reliquary print?
exam.explain: The three neighbours of P are drained before anything at distance 2 is touched, so S precedes T even though S is a dead end. That layered discipline is the queue's doing, and it is what makes the visit order and the distance order the same sequence.
exam.answer: P Q R S T U

exam.prompt: You must find the fewest hops between two accounts in an unweighted friendship graph of 10 million users. Which is the correct instrument?
exam.explain: Both traversals find *a* path in $O(V + E)$, so the choice is decided by the guarantee, not the cost. Only the FIFO frontier discovers vertices in non-decreasing distance, and only on an unweighted graph does hop count equal path cost.
choices: DFS, because recursion explores further per step and so reaches the target sooner
BFS, because a FIFO frontier discovers vertices in non-decreasing distance from the start
Either, since both visit every vertex exactly once and therefore both return the minimum
Neither: shortest paths always require sorting the vertices by degree first

exam.prompt: Write `nodesAtDistance(graph, start, d)` returning every vertex exactly `d` edges from `start`, as an array sorted with `.sort()`. Distance 0 is the start itself; an empty array when nothing sits at that distance.
exam.explain: This is BFS with the distance map kept instead of discarded, and the layer you want is just a filter over it. Note that unreachable vertices never enter the map at all, so they can never be mistaken for members of a very distant layer.
exam.hint1: Record `dist` on discovery, then keep the vertices whose distance equals d.

exam.prompt: BFS runs on the Reliquary `{ P: ["Q", "R", "S"], Q: ["P", "T"], R: ["P", "T"], S: ["P"], T: ["Q", "R", "U"], U: ["T"] }` from P. Give the final distance recorded for each vertex, as a plain number.
exam.explain: T is discovered by Q and would be discovered again by R one step later; the visited check discards that second, equal-length claim, which is why the distance map is written once per vertex and never revised. U at 3 is the eccentricity of P in this graph.

exam.prompt: A **complete** graph has an edge between every pair of its $V$ vertices. Give the worst-case time of one BFS over it in terms of $V$ alone, and derive it: how many edges does a complete graph have, what is the degree of each vertex, and which of the two terms in $O(V + E)$ dominates?
exam.explain: In a complete graph $E = V(V-1)/2$, so the $E$ term swallows the $V$ term and $O(V + E)$ collapses to $O(V^2)$. The formula has not changed; the graph has. This is exactly why the two terms must be written separately - on a sparse graph the same expression collapses the other way, to $O(V)$.

exam.prompt: Complete the depth-first traversal so that it terminates on a cyclic graph and visits each vertex once.
exam.explain: The guard must come before the mark, and the mark before the descent. Reverse either and a cycle either recurses forever or a vertex is emitted twice, which is the difference between a traversal and a walk.

exam.prompt: Write `farthestDistance(graph, start)` returning the largest BFS distance from `start` to any vertex reachable from it. A vertex with no reachable neighbours gives 0; unreachable vertices are ignored entirely.
exam.explain: This is the eccentricity of the start vertex, and BFS hands it over for free because the last layer discovered is the deepest one. Ignoring unreachable vertices is not a special case in the code: they never enter the queue, so they cannot contribute a maximum.
exam.hint1: Track a running maximum as you assign distances.

exam.prompt: A colleague argues that on a tree, which has no cycles, the visited set can be dropped from BFS to save memory. Judge that claim for a tree stored as an **undirected** adjacency list, and say when it would actually be safe.
exam.explain: In an undirected adjacency list a tree edge is stored at both ends, so a child's list contains its parent and the traversal walks straight back up: functionally a cycle of length two. Dropping the set is safe only on a rooted, directed representation where edges point one way, and even then only if no vertex has two parents.

exam.prompt: Arrange these statements into a correct argument that BFS terminates on any finite graph, from premise to conclusion.
exam.explain: Termination is a counting argument, not an appeal to the graph being acyclic. The finiteness of $V$ plus the once-only marking bounds the number of pushes, which bounds the number of iterations, so the queue must empty.
fragments: The graph has finitely many vertices V.
A vertex is pushed onto the queue only at the moment it is first marked visited.
A visited vertex is never marked again, so it is pushed at most once.
Therefore at most V pushes ever happen.
Each iteration of the while loop shifts exactly one vertex off the queue.
So the loop runs at most V times and the queue is eventually empty.

exam.prompt: This depth-first traversal returns the right answer on a path graph but crashes on the Cistern. The bug is one expression. Fix it so the function returns the recursive DFS order.
exam.explain: Handing each recursive call a brand-new visited set means nothing is ever remembered, so the A-B edge alone is enough to recurse forever until the call stack overflows. The visited set has to be one object threaded through the whole traversal; a per-call set is indistinguishable from no set at all.
exam.hint1: How many visited sets does a correct traversal create?

lesson.title: Paying Once for Work You Would Otherwise Repeat

sections.title: Two Signals: Overlapping Subproblems and Optimal Substructure
sections.body:
Dynamic programming is not a data structure or a piece of syntax - it is a **response to a shape**, and the shape announces itself with two signals.

**Overlapping subproblems**: the recursion tree asks the same question many times. Naive `fib(n)` makes $2F(n+1) - 1$ calls, which grows like $\varphi^n$ - exponential - even though only $n+1$ distinct questions exist.

**Optimal substructure**: an optimal answer to the whole is assembled from optimal answers to its parts, so a part can be solved once and reused without knowing which caller will want it.

One signal alone is not enough. Merge sort has optimal substructure but its halves never overlap, so caching them buys nothing - that is the test to run before reaching for a table.

annotations.text: A counter, not a timer - cost measured in calls is the same number on every machine.
Each call spawns two more and the tree is n deep, which is where the exponent comes from.
Ten more steps of n multiplies the work by more than a hundred: 177 calls at n=10, 21891 at n=20.

checkpoint.prompt: What does this program print? The first line is the value, the second is the number of calls made.
checkpoint.explain: Fifteen calls to answer six distinct questions ($n = 0 \ldots 5$) is the overlap made visible - the count is exactly $2F(6) - 1$. It is that ratio of calls to distinct subproblems, not the raw count, that predicts whether a table will pay for itself.

sections.title: Top-Down: Memoise the Recursion You Already Wrote
sections.body:
**Memoisation** keeps the recursive shape and adds one table: before computing, look the argument up; after computing, store it. The recurrence you wrote first is the code that ships.

The cost argument is a counting argument, not an intuition. Every distinct `n` is computed **once**, because the second visit returns from the memo before recursing, so with $n+1$ subproblems and $O(1)$ work each the running time falls from exponential to $O(n)$ - paid for with $O(n)$ table space and $O(n)$ stack depth.

Use `n in memo`, never `if (memo[n])`: `memo[0]` is `0`, which is falsy, so a truthiness test quietly refuses to believe the base case was ever cached.

annotations.text: The cache hit is the whole optimisation - it returns before the two recursive calls, pruning an entire subtree.
Compute, then store, then return - and both calls must receive this same memo object.
49 calls at n=25, where the naive version needed 242785 - and the count is exactly 2n-1.

checkpoint.prompt: What does this program print? The first line is `fib(6)`, the second is the number of calls made.
checkpoint.explain: Eleven is $2 \cdot 6 - 1$: one call opens each level on the way down, and each level makes one extra call that lands on a memo hit instead of opening a subtree. Linear rather than exponential, from a one-line change to the recursion.

sections.title: Bottom-Up: Tabulation, Then Throwing the Table Away
sections.body:
**Tabulation** turns the recurrence around. Instead of asking for `fib(n)` and letting it descend, fill `dp[0]` and `dp[1]` and sweep upwards - by the time the loop needs `dp[i - 1]` it is already written.

Same $O(n)$ time, same $O(n)$ space, but no recursion: no stack to overflow and no call overhead. The order of the sweep is what now guarantees dependencies are ready, doing the job the call stack used to do.

Then look at what the loop actually reads: only `dp[i - 1]` and `dp[i - 2]`. Everything older is dead weight, so two variables carry the whole computation and space drops to $O(1)$. That reduction is available whenever the recurrence has a **fixed, bounded window** of back-references, and it is lost the moment you need to reconstruct the path rather than the value.

annotations.text: i-1 and i-2 are already filled because the sweep is increasing. This ordering is the correctness argument.
next is computed before prev is overwritten, or the sum would lose the operand it still needs.
Both agree at n=50. The table needed 51 slots; the rolling version needed two.

checkpoint.prompt: Fill the blanks so the rolling version prints `55`.
checkpoint.explain: The temporary exists purely to break a dependency: `prev` must be read into `next` before it is overwritten, and only then does `prev` take the old `curr`. Assign in the other order and the two variables collapse onto one value, so the sequence doubles instead of adding.

sections.title: Two More Shapes: Stairs and Coins
sections.body:
**Climbing stairs** - how many ways to reach step $n$ in strides of 1 or 2 - is Fibonacci wearing a hat. The last stride came from $n-1$ or from $n-2$, so `dp[n] = dp[n-1] + dp[n-2]`, with `dp[0] = 1` because doing nothing is one way to stand on step zero.

**Coin change** is the first genuinely new shape. `dp[a]` is the fewest coins making exactly `a`, and the recurrence tries every denomination as the **last** coin: `dp[a] = 1 + min(dp[a - c])` over all `c <= a`.

Unreachable amounts must start at `Infinity`, never `0` - a zero would look like a free perfect answer and poison every larger amount built on it. The table holds `amount + 1` entries and each scans `m` denominations, so the cost is $O(n \cdot m)$ time and $O(n)$ space, where $n$ is the amount itself.

annotations.text: dp[0] = 1, not 0: the empty sequence of strides is a way of standing on step 0.
Infinity is the identity for a minimisation - it loses to every real candidate and survives only where nothing works.
The guard c <= a keeps the index in range; comparing before assigning keeps the running minimum.

checkpoint.prompt: Trace `minCoins([1, 5, 6], 11)` from the lesson code. Give the final value of each named table entry as a number.
checkpoint.explain: dp[4] is 4 because only pennies reach it, while dp[11] is 2 because the 5 and the 6 combine exactly. The table earns its keep by never committing: on `[1, 3, 4]` at 6 a greedy grab at the largest coin takes 4 and then two 1s for three coins, where comparing every choice of last coin finds 3+3.

guided-practice.prompt: What does this program print? Each line is a value followed by the number of calls that produced it.
guided-practice.explain: One extra step of `n` multiplied the work by about 1.618 - the golden ratio - because the call count is exactly $2F(n+1) - 1$ and Fibonacci itself grows geometrically. A cost that multiplies by a constant per unit of input is what exponential means, and it is why n=50 is unreachable this way.
guided-practice.hint: The call count for fib(n) is 2F(n+1) - 1, where F is the Fibonacci sequence itself.

guided-practice.prompt: Trace `climbStairs(6)` using the lesson's tabulated version (`dp[0] = 1`, `dp[1] = 1`, then `dp[i] = dp[i-1] + dp[i-2]`). Give each entry as a number.
guided-practice.explain: The row is Fibonacci shifted by one, which is the point: stairs and Fibonacci share a recurrence and differ only in base case, so one table serves both. Filling left to right means every entry is read only after it is written, and that ordering is precisely what replaces the recursive call stack.

guided-practice.prompt: State the worst-case time complexity of the naive recursive `fib(n)` with no memo, in terms of `n`, and justify it from the shape of the recursion tree. Write the answer in the form `O(2^n)`.
guided-practice.explain: Each call makes two more and the tree is n deep, so the node count is bounded above by $2^n$ and in truth grows like $\varphi^n \approx 1.618^n$ - both exponential, with $O(2^n)$ a correct if loose upper bound. The gap between $\varphi^n$ nodes and only $n+1$ distinct arguments is exactly the waste that memoisation removes.

guided-practice.prompt: Complete the memoised Fibonacci so it prints `102334155` immediately instead of grinding for hours.
guided-practice.explain: Both recursive calls must be handed the **same** table; a fresh `{}` in either position still returns the right number while leaving the cost exponential, which is the hardest class of bug to notice. `in` is used rather than a truthiness test because `memo[0]` is `0` and would otherwise never count as cached.

guided-practice.prompt: Binary search on a sorted array halves the problem and recurses into one side only. Explain whether memoising it would speed it up, and name which of the two dynamic-programming signals it fails.
guided-practice.explain: Binary search visits each subproblem exactly once - the ranges it examines are nested and never repeat - so a cache would record nothing but misses and add pure overhead. Optimal substructure is present; overlap is not, and both signals are required before a table can pay for itself.

debugging.prompt: `fib` is meant to be memoised. `fib(0)` and `fib(1)` work, but `fib(30)` throws `call budget exceeded` - the harness allows 200 calls and this makes vastly more. The recurrence and the base case are both correct. Fix the memoisation without touching `tick`.
debugging.hint: Look at what each recursive call receives as its second argument.
debugging.explain: Every recursive call was handed a brand-new empty table, so entries were written into objects discarded the moment the call returned and no lookup ever hit - the answers stayed correct while the cost stayed exponential. That is why the budget guard exists: a memo bug that returns wrong numbers is caught in a minute, and a memo bug that returns right numbers slowly is the one that reaches production.

debugging.prompt: This space-optimised `fibRolling(n)` should return the nth Fibonacci number, so `fibRolling(10)` is `55`, but it returns `512`. The base cases and loop bounds are correct. Fix the update.
debugging.hint: After the first assignment runs, what two numbers does prev + curr actually add together?
