debugging.explain: Overwriting `prev` first destroys the older value the sum still needs, so `prev + curr` degenerates into `curr + curr` and the sequence doubles - 512 is $2^9$, not a Fibonacci number. Rolling two variables is only safe when the new value is computed while both old ones are still readable, which is exactly what the temporary buys.

debugging.prompt: `climbStairs(n)` counts the ways to climb `n` stairs in strides of 1 or 2. `climbStairs(0)` and `climbStairs(1)` return `1`, but `climbStairs(5)` returns `undefined` instead of `8`. Fix the sweep.
debugging.hint: Which is the last index the loop writes, and which index does the return statement read?
debugging.explain: A tabulated solution lives on a contract between the sweep and the read: the loop must write every index the answer depends on, and `i < n` stops one short of `dp[n]`. The `undefined` is the honest symptom of an entry that was never written, and the small inputs hid it because those answers come from the base cases alone.

implementation.prompt: Write `minCoins(coins, amount)` returning the fewest coins summing to exactly `amount`, or `-1` if no combination does. Coins may be reused without limit. `minCoins([1, 3, 4], 6)` is `2`, `minCoins([2], 3)` is `-1`, and `minCoins([5, 7], 0)` is `0`.
implementation.hint: For each amount a, try every coin c <= a as the last coin and keep the smallest dp[a - c] + 1.
implementation.explain: Greedy fails on `[1, 3, 4]` at 6 - it takes the 4 and then needs two 1s, three coins where 3+3 is two - because committing to the largest coin can strand the remainder. The table never commits: at every amount it compares all choices of last coin, which is the optimal-substructure argument written out as a loop.

implementation.prompt: Write `countWays(coins, amount)` returning how many distinct **combinations** of coins sum to `amount`, where order does not matter, so 1+2 and 2+1 count as one. `countWays([1, 2, 5], 5)` is `4` and `countWays([3], 0)` is `1`.
implementation.hint: Put the loop over denominations on the outside and the loop over amounts on the inside.
implementation.explain: The loop order carries the entire meaning here. Denominations on the outside means every combination is counted in one fixed coin order, so 1+2 and 2+1 collapse into a single entry; swap the loops and the same recurrence counts **permutations** instead. Nothing about the formula changed - only the traversal decided which question you answered.

implementation.prompt: Write `tribonacci(n)` for $T(0) = 0$, $T(1) = T(2) = 1$ and $T(k) = T(k-1) + T(k-2) + T(k-3)$, using $O(1)$ extra space - no array and no memo object. `tribonacci(10)` is `149` and `tribonacci(25)` is `1389537`.
implementation.hint: Three rolling variables, and compute the new value before shifting any of them.
implementation.explain: The window of back-references is three wide instead of two, so the same reduction applies with one more variable: the space a recurrence truly needs is the width of its window, not the size of its input. The shift must happen after the sum is computed, or the oldest value is destroyed while it is still an operand.

exam.prompt: A recursive solution is a candidate for dynamic programming when it has which pair of properties?
choices: Overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure
Tail recursion and a single base case
Logarithmic depth and a sorted input
Optimal substructure and disjoint subproblems
exam.explain: The last option describes divide and conquer, not dynamic programming - disjoint subproblems are exactly the case where a cache never hits. Both signals are needed: overlap is what makes caching worth doing, and optimal substructure is what makes reusing a stored sub-answer correct regardless of which caller asked.

exam.prompt: Select every true statement about top-down memoisation compared with bottom-up tabulation on the same recurrence.
choices: Memoisation consumes call-stack depth that tabulation does not
Tabulation may compute entries that memoisation would never reach
Memoisation changes the asymptotic time complexity relative to tabulation
Tabulation makes the rolling-window space reduction easy to see
Memoisation requires the subproblems to be solved in a known order
exam.explain: Both visit each distinct subproblem once, so the asymptotic time matches; the genuine trade is stack depth and laziness against sweep order. Memoisation needs no ordering at all - the recursion discovers its own dependencies - which is why it is the easier conversion whenever a correct fill order is awkward to state up front.

exam.prompt: What does this program print? Each line is a value followed by a call count.
exam.explain: Identical answers, a 68-fold difference in work, and a gap that widens without bound as n grows - 1973 is $2F(16) - 1$ while 29 is $2 \cdot 15 - 1$. The memo changed nothing about the recurrence; it changed how many times each distinct subproblem was permitted to be evaluated.

exam.prompt: Arrange these fragments into a working tabulated `climbStairs(n)` that returns `1` for `n = 0` and `13` for `n = 6`.
fragments: for (let i = 2; i <= n; i++) dp[i] = dp[i - 1] + dp[i - 2];
exam.explain: Base cases before the sweep, sweep before the read - that dependency chain is the only ordering constraint, and satisfying it is what makes a bottom-up solution correct without any recursion to enforce it. `[1, 1]` seeds both base cases at once, and for n of 0 or 1 the loop simply never runs.

exam.prompt: Trace the lesson's `fibRolling(7)`. It starts with `prev = 0` and `curr = 1` and loops `i` from 2 to 7. After each iteration give the two variables in the form `prev,curr` - for example `0,1`.
exam.explain: The pair is a sliding window over the sequence: after iteration `i` it holds $F(i-1)$ and $F(i)$, an invariant you can state before writing the loop and check after every pass. The full $O(n)$ table was never needed because nothing in this recurrence looks back further than two.

exam.prompt: Give the worst-case time complexity of the tabulated `minCoins(coins, amount)`, where `n` is the amount and `m` is the number of denominations. Write it in the form `O(n*m)`, justify it from the loop structure, and state the space cost.
exam.explain: One entry per amount, one scan of the denominations per entry: the nested loops multiply to $O(nm)$ time with $O(n)$ space for the table. This is **pseudo-polynomial** - the cost is linear in the numeric value of the amount, not in the number of digits used to write it, so adding one digit multiplies the work by ten.

exam.prompt: Prove that coin change has optimal substructure. Let $C(a)$ be the fewest coins summing to $a$, and suppose some optimal solution for $a$ uses a coin of denomination $c$; show its remaining coins form an optimal solution for $a - c$. Use a cut-and-paste (exchange) argument, then explain why this licenses the recurrence $C(a) = 1 + \min_c C(a - c)$.
exam.explain: The argument is by contradiction: if the remainder were not optimal, swapping in a better solution for $a - c$ and re-adding the coin $c$ would beat a solution already assumed optimal, which is impossible. That is precisely what makes it safe to store one number per subproblem - the quality of a sub-answer does not depend on which larger problem asked for it, and without that property a cached value could be right for one caller and wrong for another.

exam.prompt: A colleague memoises a function that reads a mutable global configuration object as well as its argument, keying the cache on the argument alone. Explain what goes wrong, and state the property a function must have before its results may be cached.
exam.explain: A cache is a standing claim that the arguments determine the result; a hidden input breaks that claim, and the table then serves answers computed under conditions that no longer hold. Purity - or at minimum keying on every input that can change the answer - is the precondition, which is the same reason dynamic programming is always stated over values rather than over mutable state.

exam.prompt: Write the **top-down memoised** `minCoinsTopDown(coins, amount)`. The inner `best(rest)` must return the fewest coins summing to `rest`, or `Infinity` when impossible, and must consult `memo` before recursing; the outer function converts `Infinity` to `-1`. `minCoinsTopDown([1, 5, 10, 25], 300)` is `12` and must finish instantly.
exam.hint: Check `rest in memo` first, recurse on rest - c for every usable coin, and store the minimum before returning it.
exam.explain: Without the memo this recursion branches m ways to depth n and is hopeless at 300; with it, each of the 301 subproblems is evaluated once and the same recurrence runs in $O(nm)$. The memo must record `Infinity` as well - an unreachable amount is a real answer worth caching, and skipping it means re-exploring the same dead ends forever.

exam.prompt: `solve(coinSets, amount)` answers `minCoins` for several coin sets at the same amount. `solve([[1, 3, 4], [2], [5]], 6)` should be `[2, 3, -1]` but returns `[2, 2, 2]`. Fix the caching.
exam.hint: What identifies a subproblem here - the amount alone, or the amount together with the coin set?
exam.explain: A cache key must name every input the answer depends on, and this one omitted the coin set, so answers computed for `[1, 3, 4]` were handed to a caller holding `[2]`. Scoping the cache inside `minCoins` fixes it by making each top-level call its own universe; keying on the denominations plus the amount is the alternative, and it is the one to reach for when reuse across calls is genuinely wanted.

sections.title: What Makes a Greedy Choice Safe
sections.body:
A **greedy** algorithm commits to the choice that looks best right now and never reconsiders it. That is only correct when two properties hold: the **greedy-choice property** - some optimal solution begins with the greedy pick - and **optimal substructure** - after removing that pick, what remains is the same problem on a smaller input.

Both have to be argued, not assumed. Greedy coin change on $\{1,5,10,25\}$ works because every optimal solution can be rewritten to take the largest coin first; nothing in the code tells you that.

The payoff is cost. One pass with no backtracking is $O(n)$ after a sort, against exponential search over subsets.

annotations.text: Take the biggest coin as many times as it fits - the choice is never revisited, which is what makes this greedy.
Returning null rather than looping: a greedy run can end holding a remainder it cannot pay.

checkpoint.prompt: Design `maxItemsUnderBudget(prices, budget)`: return the largest number of items you can buy without the total exceeding the budget. Decide the greedy order yourself. Nothing is given to you.
checkpoint.explain: Cheapest-first is safe here because the objective counts items, not value: any set of k items costs at least as much as the k cheapest, so if the greedy prefix will not fit, no set of that size fits either.

sections.title: The Exchange Argument
sections.body:
The standard proof that a greedy rule is safe is the **exchange argument**. Take any optimal solution $O$, find the first place it disagrees with the greedy solution $G$, and show the greedy choice can be swapped into $O$ without making it worse.

Repeating the swap turns $O$ into $G$ one step at a time, so $G$ is optimal too. For **interval scheduling** - pick as many pairwise non-overlapping intervals as possible - the greedy rule is *earliest finishing time first*, and the exchange is: replacing $O$'s first interval by the one that finishes soonest can only leave more room for the rest.

Note what is not proved: that greedy finds the same solution as $O$. Only that it finds one just as good.

annotations.text: Sorting by finishing time, not by start or by length - the sort key is the whole algorithm.
Compatible means starting no earlier than the last chosen finish, so touching intervals are allowed.

checkpoint.prompt: Design `firstToFinish(intervals)`: each interval is a `[start, end]` pair. Return the interval that finishes soonest, breaking ties towards the earlier position in the input, or `null` for an empty array. Nothing is given to you.
checkpoint.explain: The strict `<` is what keeps a tie on the earlier interval, and this quantity is exactly what the exchange argument turns on: the earliest finish leaves the widest remaining window, so swapping it in never costs a later interval.

sections.title: Where Greedy Falls Apart
sections.body:
Change the coin system to $\{1, 3, 4\}$ and ask for $6$. Greedy takes $4$ and can then only pay the rest in ones, for three coins; the optimum is $3 + 3$, two coins.

Nothing is wrong with the code - the greedy-choice property simply fails for this coin set, because taking the largest coin destroys a better pairing. One counterexample is enough to kill a greedy rule, which is why hunting for one is the first thing to try.

When greedy fails you fall back to searching the options, which costs vastly more. **Proving safety is what buys the speed.**

annotations.text: The exhaustive version tries every coin at every step - correct for any coin set, and exponential in the amount.
Prints 3 2: greedy is wrong at 6. The next line prints 2 2, so a passing example proves nothing.

checkpoint.prompt: Design `greedyCoinCount(coins, amount)`: take the largest usable coin repeatedly and return how many coins that used, or `-1` if the greedy run ends with a remainder it cannot pay. Nothing is given to you.
checkpoint.explain: The `[2, 4], 5` case matters most: greedy does not merely return a worse answer, it returns none at all. Telling 'greedy got stuck' apart from 'no combination exists' needs the exhaustive version, which is precisely what greedy refused to do.

sections.title: Dijkstra Without a Priority Queue
sections.body:
**Dijkstra** grows a set of settled vertices. Each round it settles the unsettled vertex with the smallest tentative distance - a greedy choice - then **relaxes** every edge leaving it: if `dist[u] + w` beats `dist[v]`, record the better route.

That choice is safe because weights are non-negative: any other route to that vertex must leave the settled set through some unsettled vertex that is already at least as far away, and extending it only adds more. This is also exactly why a negative edge breaks Dijkstra.

Without a heap, finding the minimum is a **linear scan** over all $V$ vertices, once per round: $O(V^2)$ of scanning plus $O(E)$ relaxations, and since $E \le V^2$ that is $O(V^2)$ overall. A binary heap trades this for $O((V + E)\log V)$, which only wins on sparse graphs.

annotations.text: This inner loop is the missing priority queue: V comparisons per round, V rounds, hence the V-squared term.
No reachable unsettled vertex remains, so everything still at Infinity is unreachable and the loop can stop early.
Relaxation. Each directed edge is examined exactly once, in the round its tail is settled - that is the O(E) term.

checkpoint.prompt: Design `closestUnvisited(dist, visited)`: `dist` maps vertex names to numbers, `visited` is an array of names already settled. Return the unvisited vertex with the smallest distance, breaking ties towards the earlier key, or `null` when every vertex is visited. Nothing is given to you.
checkpoint.explain: This single helper is the entire cost story of heap-free Dijkstra: called once per round, reading every vertex, so V rounds times V reads gives the V-squared term. The strict `<` also fixes the tie-break, which is what keeps the settle order deterministic.

unseen-challenge.prompt: Design `scheduleMax(intervals)`: each interval is a `[start, end]` pair, and intervals that merely touch - one ending exactly where the next begins - are compatible. Return the size of the largest set of pairwise non-overlapping intervals. Nothing is given to you.
unseen-challenge.explain: Sorting by finish is the whole design; the scan afterwards is trivial. The first case punishes a start-time rule, since [0, 7] starts earliest and alone blocks two compatible intervals, and the last punishes a shortest-first rule.

unseen-challenge.prompt: Design `minCoins(coins, amount)`: return the fewest coins that make the amount exactly, or `-1` when no combination does. Greedy is not good enough here - your answer must be optimal for every coin set. Amounts stay under 100. Nothing is given to you.
unseen-challenge.explain: Every amount has to consider every coin, because the choice that looks worst locally is the one that wins at 6. The price of correctness on an arbitrary coin set is O(amount x coins) work instead of a single pass - that gap is what a safety proof buys you when greedy does hold.

unseen-challenge.prompt: Design `dijkstra(graph, source)`. `graph` maps each vertex name to an array of `[neighbour, weight]` pairs with non-negative weights, and every neighbour is itself a key. Return an object mapping every vertex to its shortest distance from the source, using `null` for unreachable vertices. Find the minimum by linear scan - no heap. Nothing is given to you.
unseen-challenge.explain: The fourth graph separates a real implementation from a hop-counting walk: the direct edge A-B of weight 4 loses to the two-hop route through C, so B must not be settled before C. Unreachable vertices stay at Infinity forever, which is why the scan has to skip them instead of picking one and relaxing from nowhere.

unseen-challenge.prompt: You run the heap-free Dijkstra on a graph with $V$ vertices and $E$ directed edges stored as adjacency lists. State the worst-case running time as a single big-O in $V$, and justify the two costs - finding the minimum and relaxing - separately.
unseen-challenge.explain: Two costs add: V rounds each scanning V vertices for the minimum gives V^2, while every adjacency list is walked exactly once for E relaxations in total, so the honest bound is O(V^2 + E). Since E is at most V^2 in a simple graph the sum collapses to O(V^2) - relaxation is never the bottleneck here, which is exactly why a heap only pays off when the graph is sparse.

unseen-challenge.prompt:
Trace the heap-free Dijkstra from `A` on this graph, where each entry lists `[neighbour, weight]`:

- `A: [[B, 4], [C, 1]]`
- `B: [[D, 1]]`
- `C: [[B, 2], [D, 5]]`
- `D: [[E, 3]]`
- `E: []`

Write `inf` for a distance that is still infinite.

steps.label: tentative distances to B, C, D, E after settling A
the second vertex settled, and its final distance
tentative distance to B immediately after C is settled
the order in which all five vertices are settled

unseen-challenge.explain: B is the vertex worth watching: it sits at 4 after the first round and drops to 3 once C is settled, which is legal only because B was still unsettled. D likewise improves from 6 to 4. Once a vertex is settled its distance is frozen, and with non-negative weights nothing later can beat it.

exam.prompt: What does this print?
exam.answer:
5: greedy=2 best=2
6: greedy=3 best=2
7: greedy=2 best=2
8: greedy=2 best=2
exam.explain: Three of the four amounts agree, and that is the point: a greedy rule can be right on nearly every input and still be wrong. Only 6 exposes it, because committing to 4 destroys the 3 + 3 pairing.

exam.prompt: Design `minRoomsNeeded(intervals)`: given `[start, end]` meeting times, return the fewest rooms that can host all of them, where a meeting ending at time t and one starting at t may share a room. Nothing is given to you.
exam.explain: The answer is the largest number of meetings alive at one instant, and sweeping the sorted start and end times finds it without ever assigning a meeting to a named room. Comparing with `<` rather than `<=` is what lets a meeting reuse a room freed at exactly that moment.

exam.prompt: You have invented a greedy rule for a new problem and it gives the right answer on twenty test cases. Say what is still missing, and describe the shape of the argument that would settle it.
exam.explain: Passing tests can only fail to find a counterexample; it never establishes the greedy-choice property. The exchange argument closes the gap: take an arbitrary optimal solution, find the first choice where it differs from greedy, show the greedy choice can be swapped in without loss, and repeat until the optimum has become the greedy answer.

exam.prompt: Give the worst-case running time of earliest-finish-first interval scheduling on $n$ intervals, assuming a comparison sort, and justify which part of the algorithm dominates.
exam.explain: The greedy part is one O(n) scan; sorting by finishing time dominates at O(n log n). That is typical of greedy algorithms - almost all the work goes into imposing the right order, after which each decision is a single comparison against the last commitment.

exam.prompt: Trace earliest-finish-first on these intervals: `[1, 4]`, `[3, 5]`, `[0, 6]`, `[5, 7]`, `[3, 9]`, `[6, 10]`, `[8, 11]`. Touching intervals are compatible. Write intervals as `[a, b]` and separate a list with commas.

steps.label: the intervals in the order the sort produces
the value of lastEnd after that first choice

exam.explain: [0, 6] is the rejection that matters: it starts earliest of all, so a start-time greedy would have taken it and lost [1, 4] and [5, 7] both. Sorting by finish keeps lastEnd as small as possible after every commitment, which is the invariant the exchange argument exploits.

exam.prompt: Design `shortestPath(graph, source, target)`. `graph` maps each vertex to an array of `[neighbour, weight]` pairs with non-negative weights. Return the vertex names along a shortest path from source to target as an array, `[source]` when they are the same vertex, and `[]` when the target is unreachable. Nothing is given to you.
exam.explain: Distances alone name no route, so every successful relaxation must also record who caused it; walking those predecessors back from the target and reversing rebuilds the path. The unreachable case has to be checked before that walk, since an untouched vertex has no predecessor to follow.

exam.prompt: Prove that earliest-finish-first selects a maximum-size set of pairwise compatible intervals. Argue by exchange against an arbitrary optimal solution.
exam.explain: The engine of the proof is that greedy's k-th choice finishes no later than the optimal solution's k-th choice, by induction: if that holds through k, the optimal (k+1)-th interval is still compatible with greedy's prefix, so greedy's own pick finishes no later still. Greedy therefore never runs out of room first, and its set is at least as large - which shows equal size, never that the two sets are identical.

exam.prompt: Why does a single negative-weight edge break Dijkstra, even on a graph with no negative cycle?
choices: The distance array would hold negative numbers, which the comparison mishandles
Settling a vertex assumes no later route can be shorter, and a negative edge can falsify that
The linear scan cannot find a minimum among negative values
Relaxation would never terminate
exam.explain: Dijkstra's greedy choice rests entirely on monotonicity - extending a path never shortens it - so the nearest unsettled vertex must already be final. A negative edge lets a longer prefix end up cheaper, and by then the vertex was frozen and is never revisited.

exam.prompt: Complete the relaxation step of Dijkstra for the edge from `u` to `v` with weight `w`.
exam.explain: Relaxation may only ever lower a distance, so the comparison is the strict one; the assignment must recompute the sum rather than copy `dist[u]`, because the route to v costs the route to u plus the edge.

exam.prompt: Put one round of heap-free Dijkstra into the order it must happen.
fragments: scan every unsettled vertex and take the one with the smallest tentative distance
mark that vertex settled - its distance is now final
walk its adjacency list, one edge at a time
if dist[u] + w beats dist[v], lower dist[v]
exam.explain: Settling before relaxing is what makes the algorithm terminate: the settled vertex leaves the scan for good, so exactly V rounds finish the graph. Relaxing an edge back into an already settled vertex is also what a negative weight would need to do, and cannot.

exam.prompt: Interval scheduling and heap-free Dijkstra both make a locally best choice and never take it back. Explain what plays the role of the exchange argument in Dijkstra: what property of the input makes settling the nearest unsettled vertex safe?
exam.explain: Any rival route to the nearest unsettled vertex must first leave the settled set through some other unsettled vertex whose tentative distance is already at least as large, and non-negative weights mean the remainder of that route only adds to it. So no cheaper route can exist and the vertex may be frozen - the same swap-in-the-greedy-choice shape as the interval proof, resting on monotonicity rather than on finishing times.

exam.prompt: Design `canFinishAll(jobs, deadline)`: each job is a positive duration, the jobs run one after another on a single machine, and you may choose the order. Return `true` if some order finishes every job by the deadline, measuring finish times from time zero. Nothing is given to you.
exam.explain: The design insight is that the ordering is irrelevant here: the last job always finishes at the total duration, so every permutation ties and the greedy question dissolves into a sum. Recognising that a choice cannot matter is as much a part of design as proving that one is safe.

sections.title: Text Becomes Terms
sections.body:
A search engine never searches text. It searches **terms**, and `tokenise` is the one function that decides what a term is: lowercase everything, cut at every run of characters that is not a letter or a digit, and throw the empty pieces away.

That single decision is the engine's entire vocabulary. `Cat`, `CAT` and `cat,` must collapse to the same term or a query for `cat` misses two documents in three, and the **query is tokenised by the same function** so that both sides of the comparison speak one language.

The rule is deliberately crude - `Don't` becomes `don` and `t`, and `mats` never meets `mat` - which is exactly why real engines add a stemmer. Crude is survivable; **inconsistent is not**, because an index built one way and queried another silently returns nothing at all.

annotations.text: Lowercase first, then split. Doing it the other way round means writing the case rule twice.
Splitting on a run of non-alphanumerics collapses "mat.  The" into two pieces rather than four, but a leading or trailing separator still yields an empty string - hence the filter.
The apostrophe is a separator like any other, so this prints don and t as two terms. Deterministic, and visibly imperfect.
Whitespace only: split gives two empty strings, the filter removes both, and the answer is an empty array rather than [""].
Duplicates are kept. Term frequency is about to need that count.

checkpoint.prompt: Write `tokenise(text)`. Lowercase the text, split it on every run of characters that is not `a-z` or `0-9`, and return the non-empty pieces in order. Duplicates are kept.
checkpoint.explain: Tokenising is a normalisation, not a clean-up: its job is to guarantee that one word written two ways lands on one term, so that a document and a query can be compared at all. The empty-string filter is the part people forget - splitting on a leading or trailing separator hands back "", and an empty term in a postings list would match every document containing a full stop.

sections.title: The Inverted Index
sections.body:
A forward index maps a document to its terms, which is precisely the wrong direction: answering `cat` would mean reading every document in the corpus. An **inverted index** maps a term to the documents that contain it, with a count - the term's **postings list**.

Building it is one pass. Each of the $n$ tokens in the corpus is read once and incremented into one posting, so construction is $O(n)$ in the total token count, and the index is then reused by every query that follows.

Two more things must be stored alongside the postings: the **number of documents** $N$, which the IDF will need, and each document's **length** in tokens, which the term frequency will need. A term nobody wrote has no posting at all, so a lookup yields `undefined` rather than an empty object - guard it, or counting its postings throws.

annotations.text: documentCount is captured here, at build time. Recomputing it later from the postings is wrong - a document containing no terms at all still counts.
The length is the token count including duplicates, which is what makes tf a proportion of the document rather than of its vocabulary.
Create the posting on first sight of the term. This one line is why the whole build stays a single pass.
The || 0 handles the first occurrence in this document; every later one simply increments.
"the" appears twice in a and once in b, so the posting carries counts, not merely membership.
An unseen term is undefined, not {}. Every reader of postings has to expect that.

checkpoint.prompt: The four documents below are indexed in order. After each one, give the **postings list for the term `the`** exactly as it stands - written `{docId:count, ...}` with the ids in the order they were first added, or `{}` if it has none yet.
checkpoint.explain: Document c is the step that teaches the structure: it is indexed in full, it lengthens the corpus and it raises $N$ - and it leaves this postings list untouched, because it contains no `the`. That is the whole point of inverting the index. A query for `the` never looks at c at all, so the cost of answering it is the length of this list rather than the size of the corpus.

sections.title: Weighing a Term: TF-IDF
sections.body:
Counting matches ranks long documents first, and ranks a document that says `the` forty times above one that is actually about cats. **TF-IDF** repairs both halves. Term frequency divides the count by the document's length, giving a proportion rather than a total:

$$\mathrm{tf}(t,d) = \frac{\mathrm{count}(t,d)}{|d|}$$

Inverse document frequency asks how rare the term is across the corpus, where $N$ is the number of documents and $\mathrm{df}(t)$ is how many of them contain $t$. We use the **natural logarithm**, `Math.log`, and saying so is not pedantry - a different base rescales every score in the engine, and a ranking is only reproducible once the base is pinned:

$$\mathrm{idf}(t) = \ln\frac{N}{\mathrm{df}(t)}$$

A term's weight in a document is $\mathrm{tf} \times \mathrm{idf}$, and two boundary cases fall straight out of the formula. A term in **every** document has $\mathrm{df} = N$, so $\ln 1 = 0$ and it contributes nothing - the stop-word list you never had to write - and a term in **no** document would divide by zero, so define its IDF as $0$ rather than let an infinity into the sort.

annotations.text: A length of zero would divide by zero, and an unknown document id gives undefined - one guard covers both.
df is just the size of the postings list. Nothing else has to be scanned to know it.
df === 0 is the unseen term. Returning 0 keeps NaN and Infinity out of the ranking.
cat is rarer than the, and c is shorter than a - both effects push c above a.
the earns 0.0959 in a document it appears in twice: high tf, feeble idf.
ln(4/4) = 0. A term everybody uses is worth exactly nothing, and no stop-word list was needed to decide it.

checkpoint.prompt: Scoring a single-term query against a finished inverted index means visiting each document in that term's postings list and computing $\mathrm{tf} \times \mathrm{idf}$ for it. State the cost in terms of $\mathrm{df}$, the number of documents containing the term, and justify it: say what the query does *not* touch, and where the corpus-sized work went.
checkpoint.explain: The corpus-sized work did not vanish - it was paid once, at build time, in the $O(n)$ pass over every token, and every query since has been amortising it. IDF adds nothing to the bill because $\mathrm{df}$ is the length of the very list being walked and $N$ was stored when the index was built, so no second pass over the documents is needed. This is the trade the inverted index exists to make: one expensive build in exchange for queries costing what the term is rare, not what the collection is large.

sections.title: Parsing the Query, Ranking the Answer
sections.body:
A query is text with **operators** in it. Splitting on whitespace first lets a leading `+` or `-` be read before the word is tokenised - `+cat mat -dog` means cat is required, mat is merely wanted, and dog disqualifies a document however well it scores otherwise.

Only the required and optional terms score; an excluded term is a filter and never a contribution. A document survives when it holds every required term, none of the excluded ones and at least one scoring term, and its score is then the sum of $\mathrm{tf} \times \mathrm{idf}$ over those scoring terms.

The sort needs a **total order** or the engine is not deterministic, and exact ties are common - a term appearing in every document scores $0$ everywhere. So: score descending, and on a tie, document id ascending. What the caller is promised is the **order**, not the numbers, which is what lets the weighting change later without breaking every test.

annotations.text: Split on whitespace, not with tokenise - tokenise would eat the + and - before they could ever be read.
The prefix is stripped, and what remains goes through tokenise, so query words are normalised exactly like document text.
One word can yield several terms once tokenised, and they all inherit that word's bucket.
The comparator falls through to the id only when the scores are equal, which makes the ordering total and the tests stable.
a and d tie at 0.1155, so the id decides: a before d, on every single run.

checkpoint.prompt: Write `parseQuery(query)` returning `{ required, optional, excluded }`. Split the query on whitespace; a word starting with `+` is required, one starting with `-` is excluded, anything else is optional. Strip the prefix, tokenise the rest, and push each resulting term into that bucket. **A term already sitting in any bucket is skipped** - first occurrence wins.
checkpoint.explain: The prefix must be read before tokenising, because tokenise treats `+` and `-` as separators and would destroy the operator on its way past. The dedupe rule is what stops `the +the` being scored twice and, worse, stops a term being required and excluded at once - a contradiction the ranking loop has no sensible answer to, settled here by a rule the caller can predict rather than by whichever loop happens to run last.

trial.prompt:
**The Trial.** Build a search engine as six pure functions. No storage, no network, no state kept between calls - the acceptance tests below are the whole specification, and nothing is hidden from you.

`tokenise(text)` lowercases the text, splits it on every run of characters outside `a-z0-9`, and returns the non-empty pieces in order, duplicates kept.

`buildIndex(documents)` takes an array of `{ id, text }` and returns exactly three keys.

- `documentCount` - how many documents were given.
- `docLengths` - `{ id: tokenCount }` for every document, counting duplicates, and `0` for a document with no terms.
- `postings` - `{ term: { id: countInThatDocument } }`, holding only the documents in which that term actually occurs. A term nobody used has no key at all.

`termFrequency(index, term, docId)` returns the count divided by that document's length, and `0` when the term, the document or the length is missing.

`inverseDocumentFrequency(index, term)` returns $\ln(N / \mathrm{df})$, where $N$ is `index.documentCount` and $\mathrm{df}$ is the size of the term's postings list. **The base is $e$ - use `Math.log`.** A term with $\mathrm{df} = 0$ returns `0`, never `Infinity`.

`parseQuery(query)` returns `{ required, optional, excluded }`, all arrays of terms. Split the query on whitespace; a word starting with `+` is required, one starting with `-` is excluded, anything else is optional. Strip that prefix, tokenise what remains, and push each term into that bucket - unless the term already sits in some bucket, in which case skip it, first occurrence winning.

`search(index, query)` returns **an array of document ids, ranked** - no scores, no objects. The scoring terms are the required ones followed by the optional ones. A document is returned when it contains every required term, contains no excluded term, and contains at least one scoring term; its score is $\sum \mathrm{tf}(t,d)\cdot\mathrm{idf}(t)$ over the scoring terms. Rank by score **descending**, breaking ties on **document id ascending** so that the order is total. A query with no scoring terms returns `[]`.

The tests call `search`, and the index they hand it is sometimes one your `buildIndex` has just made and sometimes a literal written by hand - so `search` must read the documented structure rather than rebuild it. Two tests pass an index whose document ids are facts about your other functions; those check that the pieces you were told to build exist and agree.

tests.label: search(buildIndex(corpus), "cat") ranks by tf-idf
tests.input: buildIndex([{ id: "a", text: "the cat sat on the mat" }, { id: "b", text: "a dog sat on the log" }, { id: "c", text: "cat and dog and cat" }, { id: "d", text: "the quiet mat" }]), "cat"

tests.label: search(buildIndex(corpus), "cat dog") sums both terms
tests.input: buildIndex([{ id: "a", text: "the cat sat on the mat" }, { id: "b", text: "a dog sat on the log" }, { id: "c", text: "cat and dog and cat" }, { id: "d", text: "the quiet mat" }]), "cat dog"

tests.label: the query is tokenised too: "Cat, DOG!"
tests.input: buildIndex([{ id: "a", text: "the cat sat on the mat" }, { id: "b", text: "a dog sat on the log" }, { id: "c", text: "cat and dog and cat" }, { id: "d", text: "the quiet mat" }]), "Cat, DOG!"

tests.label: search(buildIndex(corpus), "+cat -dog") filters before it ranks
tests.input: buildIndex([{ id: "a", text: "the cat sat on the mat" }, { id: "b", text: "a dog sat on the log" }, { id: "c", text: "cat and dog and cat" }, { id: "d", text: "the quiet mat" }]), "+cat -dog"

tests.label: search(buildIndex(corpus), "quiet mat") - the rare term dominates
tests.input: buildIndex([{ id: "a", text: "the cat sat on the mat" }, { id: "b", text: "a dog sat on the log" }, { id: "c", text: "cat and dog and cat" }, { id: "d", text: "the quiet mat" }]), "quiet mat"

tests.label: search(buildIndex(corpus), "+sat +on") - an exact tie breaks on id
tests.input: buildIndex([{ id: "a", text: "the cat sat on the mat" }, { id: "b", text: "a dog sat on the log" }, { id: "c", text: "cat and dog and cat" }, { id: "d", text: "the quiet mat" }]), "+sat +on"

tests.label: search reads a hand-written index it did not build
tests.input: { documentCount: 3, docLengths: { p: 10, q: 5, r: 4 }, postings: { rust: { p: 3, q: 1 }, memory: { q: 2, r: 1 } } }, "rust memory"

tests.label: search(buildIndex(corpus), "zebra") - term absent from the corpus
tests.input: buildIndex([{ id: "a", text: "the cat sat on the mat" }, { id: "b", text: "a dog sat on the log" }, { id: "c", text: "cat and dog and cat" }, { id: "d", text: "the quiet mat" }]), "zebra"

tests.label: probe: the structure buildIndex produced
probe: tokenise, tf, idf and parseQuery agree with the spec

trial.explain:
Every rule lives in exactly one function, and the pipeline runs in one direction: text becomes terms, terms become an index, the index becomes a weighting, the weighting becomes an order. That is what makes the thing testable at all. Ranking is the only part a user ever sees and the part hardest to assert on directly, so the contract is the order and the index structure rather than the floating-point scores, and the probe tests reach the interior functions through the single entry point the harness calls.

The cost model is why any of this exists. Building the index is $O(n)$ over the corpus's total tokens, paid once; a query then walks only the postings lists of the terms it mentions, so answering `zebra` across a million documents costs almost nothing, because there is no list to walk. Scanning the documents per query would instead have made every search $O(n)$ forever.

Two details separate a working engine from a plausible one. Dividing by document length stops a long document winning merely by being long, and the logarithm in IDF makes a term appearing in every document worth exactly zero - $\ln(N/N) = 0$ - so the stop-word list writes itself out of the corpus instead of out of your assumptions about English. The tie-break on id is not cosmetic either: without a total order the same query returns a different page on different runs, and neither a test nor a user can trust the result.
